59.       It was also pointed out that the Fifth Pay Commission had recommended for the Chief Commissioner a five-year
 tenure, long enough to enable him to give a sense of direction and purpose to the organisation, even if it takes his
 retirement age upto 62 years.  It was pointed out that even when Commissioners were retiring at the age of 58 years, the
 Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety was given an additional 2 years, enabling him to retire at 60 years.  Now, both
 the Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety and the Commissioners retired at the age of 60 years. 
 
60.       The Committee is constrained to note that vacancies continue to exist in the Commission of Railway Safety for
 fairly long periods because of non-availability of eligible officers from the Ministry of Railways.  The Committee
 recommends that any vacancy arising in the Commission of Railway Safety should be filled up at the earliest so that the
 functioning of the Commission does not suffer.  The Committee is also constrained to note that the recommendations
 made by Railway Safety Review Committee 1998 are yet to be implemented by the Government.  The Chief
 Commissioner of Railway Safety, being the Principal Technical Advisor to the Government of India on matters
 concerning rail safety, is the highest technical official in the Ministry of Civil Aviation for dealing with railway safety. 
 The Committee is of the view that upgradation of the post of Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety to the level of
 Secretary to the Government of India is absolutely essential so that he can effectively and forcefully interact with the
 nine Secretary level officers of Railway Board.  Lack of such a status to the Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety
 works as a serious deterrent to him in discharging his duties effectively in a hierarchy conscious bureaucracy.  The
 Committee, therefore, recommends that the status of Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety should be equal to that of
 the Chairman of Railway Board in rank and pay.  Likewise the status of Commissioner of Railway Safety should be
 equal to that of General Manager of a Zonal Railway in rank as well as pay.  The posts of Deputy Commissioners of
 Railway Safety should be manned by Senior Administration Grade Officers.   The Commissioners of Railway Safety
 should also be provided with the assistance of Deputy Commissioners. The Committee further recommends that, as
 recommended by the Fifth Central Pay Commission, the tenure of the Chief Commissioner should be five years, taking
 him beyond normal retirement age and upto 62 years.  The Committee is of the firm view that these measures would
 bring to an end the current scenario of shortage of volunteers opting to join the Commission of Railway Safety.   Also
 these measures will significantly enhance the status of the Commission, make it more dynamic and enable it to
 discharge its functions more effectively and its views heard and acted upon, with due importance by Railway
 Administration.
 
EXPOSURE TO TECHNOLOGICAL ADVANCEMENTS
61.       The Committee pointed out that a lot of technological advancements had been taking place in the railway sector
 and enquired as to how the officers of the Commissioner kept updating their technical know-how.  In response, the
 Committee was informed by the Commission of Railway Safety that while the railways were advancing in technology
 on rolling stock, locomotives, coaches, wagons, signaling systems and railway officers were frequently sent abroad to
 visit and get a first hand knowledge of the latest technologies in the working of the railways.  However, the officers of
 the Commission do not get an equal opportunity to get exposed to the technologies which were developing abroad.  The
 Committee was also informed that Railway Board has given its officers the facility to become members of five
 professional institutions including two foreign institutions.  Again, no such facilities were available to the officers of
 Commission of Railway Safety.  The Committee was also informed that the requests of the Commission to the Railway
 Board that whenever officers of the Railways are nominated for such exposure to new technologies by sending them
 abroad, the Railway Board should also include officers of the Commission in such visits, had not been acceded to by
 the Railway Board.
 
62.       The Committee brought the above point to the notice of Railway Board and sought their comments in the
 matter.  In reply, the Committee was informed by the Railway Board that the Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety
 had requested Ministry of Railways for training of his personnel in technology familiarization programmes abroad,
 alongwith other Indian Railway officers at Railways' cost.  The issue was examined and it was felt that dependence of
 the Commission on the Ministry of Railways for financial assistance will impair the independent identity of the
 Commission, and to maintain it, it is desirable that the Commission should be financially independent of Railways.  It
 would, therefore, not be possible to sponsor personnel of Commission of Railway Safety for training and technology
 familiarization programmes abroad on Railway expenses.

63.       The Committee feels that there is a genuine need of the officers of Commission of Railway Safety to get exposed
 to the latest technological advancements taking place in the railway sector in India and abroad.  Otherwise there is a
 real danger that the technical knowledge of the officers of the Commission will get obsolete.  The Committee
 recommends that the officers of the Commission should be exposed to latest technologies through trainings in the
 country and abroad, so that they are in a position to perform their role effectively.  The officers of the Commission
 should also be given full facilities to become members of professional institutions, at par with the facilities extended by
 the railway administration to railway officers.  This will help in keeping the officers of the Commission updated in their
 technical knowledge.  However, for this purpose, the Commission should not depend upon the financial assistance of
 the Ministry of Railways.  The Committee recommends that the Government should ensure that the budget of the
 Commission of Railway Safety is suitably increased so that these requirements could be taken care of by the
 Commission itself.
 
SUPPLY OF RAILWAY CIRCULARS ETC. TO COMMISSION OF RAILWAY SAFETY
64.       During the course of the evidence of the officers of Ministry of Civil Aviation and Commission of Railway
 Safety, the Committee was also informed that the Commission had to be aware of the happenings in the railway. 
 However, the Commission was not even on the permanent mailing list of Railway Board for orders/circulars affecting
 railway safety.  The Committee was further informed that the Ministry of Railways does not keep the Commission
 informed of the proceedings of various technical Committees such as Rolling Stock Committee, Signal Committee,
 Bridge Committee etc. since these Committees discuss various maintenance and safety problems encountered in day-to-
day working of the Railways.  The Commission was of the view that it would help the Commission in understanding the
 problems and steps taken to solve these problems by the Railways.  The Committee sought the comments of the
 Ministry of Railways in the above issues raised by the Commission of Railway Safety.
 
65.       Ministry of Railways informed the Committee that the Commissioner of Railway Safety is on the permanent
 mailing list of the Railway Board for all orders/circulars affecting railway safety.  As a matter of fact, copies of not
 only orders/circulars on safety, but all important policy instructions/orders/circulars etc. are endorsed to Chief
 Commissioner of Railway Safety.  Most of the recommendations of the Commission are generally accepted and
 instructions are issued, based on these accepted recommendations and information is given to the Commission of
 Railway Safety, regarding these instructions.
 
 
 
66.       As regards keeping the Commission informed of the proceedings of the various technical Committees, the
 Ministry of Railways replied that the various technical committees such as Rolling Stock Committee, Signal Committee
 etc. are internal Committees of the Railways to discuss various issues pertaining to the existing standards of the
 equipment of the concerned department i.e. Mechanical, Signal etc. and needs for their modifications.  Since the matter
 is totally technical pertaining to Signal and Mechanical Departments, etc. it shall be of no use to Commission as the
 proceedings of these committees are recommendatory in nature.  The recommendations made by these committees are
 examined in Board's Office, and if found suitable, only then policy instructions/guidelines are issued and the copies of
 such guidelines/instructions are also endorsed to Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety.
 
67.       The Committee is of the view that unless the Commission of Railway Safety is kept aware of the latest
 instructions with respect to railway safety issued by the Railway Board or Zonal Railways, it cannot discharge its duties
 effectively.  Ministry of Railways have admitted that copies of all important policy orders are endorsed to the Chief
 Commissioner of Railway Safety.  The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Railways should ensure that
 Commission of Railway Safety is on the permanent mailing list of Railway Board and Zonal Railways for all policy
 Circulars having bearing on safety and all Circulars/Orders affecting safety.  The Committee further recommends that
 the Commission of Railway Safety should be supplied with the proceeding of the Technical Committees of Railway
 Board so that the Commission remains informed of the safety problems encountered in the working of the railways and
 the measures taken to solve these problems.
 
LACK OF OFFICE INFRASTRUCTURE
68.       The Committee enquired from the Commission of Railway Safety regarding the budget allocation of the

 Commission and the office infrastructure available to it.  The Committee was informed that the overall budget
 allocation of the Commission has been satisfactory.  However taking into account the nature of work of Commissioner
 of Railway Safety, the allocations of funds for domestic travel as well as foreign travel has been totally inadequate. 
 The Commission of Railway Safety as well as Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety are required to be present at the
 accident site at the earliest for which they require air journey which is not possible in the present budget allocation. 
 They are also required to travel to Lucknow and Delhi in connection with discussions and conferences with Chief
 Commissioner of Railway Safety and RDSO at Lucknow and Railway Board and Ministry of Civil Aviation at Delhi. 
 Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety is also required to undertake extensive tours to various Zonal Railways and
 headquarters of Commissioners spread over the country in the course of discharge of his duties.  The Committee was
 also informed that the exposure of officers of Commission of Railway Safety to new technologies and systems
 practiced abroad was not being done due to lack of funds for foreign travel.  The Commission also complained of lack
 of infrastructure and proper office machinery.  It was informed that the Commission did not have sufficient official
 vehicles, mobile phones and manpower for officials in comparison to officials of same status in Ministry of Railways. 
 The Committee was further informed that Railway had earlier agreed to provide mobile phones to the Chief
 Commissioner of Railway Safety and Commissioners of Railway Safety so that in an emergency they can be reached. 
 However, the commitment had not been honoured.  In the absence of such facilities, the Commissioners find it
 impossible to contact Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety and Railway Officials quickly for conveying
 information/seeking direction after the occurrence of an accident.
 
69.       The Committee notes with concern the constraints faced by the officers of the Commission of Railway Safety in
 performing their duties due to lack of budgetary allocations and proper infrastructure and office machinery.  The
 Committee feels that the Commission of Railway Safety need adequate budgetary support from the Government so that
 it does not have to look upon the Ministry of Railways for being able to effectively discharge its duties.  The
 Committee recommends that the budget allocation of Commission of Railway Safety should be substantially increased
 so that the Commission could take care of its essential requirements such as funds for foreign training, air travel within
 India, nominations to various training courses, membership to professional institutions etc. 
 
ANNOUNCEMENT OF PRIMA-FACIE CAUSE OF ACCIDENTS BY RAILWAY ADMINISTRATION
70.       The Committee observes that whenever a train accident occurs, the railway administration is quick to announce
 the prima-facie cause of the accident, even when the officials concerned are aware of the enormity of the accident and
 that, as provided in the Railway Act, Commissioner of Railway Safety would hold an enquiry to determine the exact
 cause of the accident.  However, if at a later date, the findings of the Commissioner of Railway Safety happen to
 coincide with the version earlier advanced by the railway officials, the Commission of Railway Safety is accused of a
 bias in favour of the Railways. Such actions affect the credibility of Commissioner of Railway Safety.
 
71.       The Committee is of the opinion that the unwritten convention that no one would give the cause of an accident,
 when an enquiry is pending, needs to be followed by the Railway administration.  The Committee recommends that the
 Railway administration should refrain from speculating and giving the prime-facie cause of an accident, which is
 required to be statutorily enquired by the Commissioner of Railway Safety.  This will ensure that the credibility of the
 Commission of Railway Safety is maintained and the Commissioners are not suspected of prejudice or bias in
 conducting their enquiries.
 
CONCLUSION
72.       The Committee is of the opinion that the Commission of Railway Safety is an important organisation of the
 Government and, in the prevailing circumstances, the Commission's hands need strengthening in all possible ways. The
 Committee recommends that the Government should bring a comprehensive legislation incorporating the suggestion
 made by the Committee in this Report so that the functioning of the Commission of Railway Safety could improve in
 the interest of the public travelling by Indian Railways.

 the Commission of Railway Safety, it is essential that the Commission works outside the control of both the Ministries

 Union Public Service Commission.  The Committee also agrees with the contention of the Ministry of Railways that
 officers below the rank of Commissioner of Railway Safety should also not be sent on deputation, rather they should go
 on absorption terms to the Commission.   The Committee is of the firm view that this would make the Commission
 independent, powerful and vigilant to the fullest extent.   This would definitely go a long way in dispelling the general
 impression that the Ministry of Railways unduly influences the Commission in its functioning as it is rightly said that
 justice should not only be done but it should also appear to have been done.

EFFECTIVENESS OF RECOMMENDATIONS OF COMMISSION OF RAILWAY SAFETY
 
The Committee is of the view that although the recommendations of the Commission of Railway Safety are not
 mandatory for the Ministry of Railways yet the situation brought out by the Commission of Railway Safety is highly
 unsatisfactory.  The Committee is of the view that the recommendations made by the Commission of Railway Safety
 should receive utmost importance from the Ministry of Railways.  The Committee takes exception to the fact that, on
 certain occasions, the Ministry of Railways neither consults the Commission of Railway Safety before rejecting a
 recommendation nor furnishes reasons for not accepting the recommendations made by the Commission of Railway
 Safety.  The Committee strongly feels that the Commission of Railway Safety is a watch dog on behalf of the public at
 large.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Railways, should honour the commitment made by
 them to the Appointment Committee of Cabinet regarding consulting the Commission before rejecting a
 recommendation.   The Committee further recommends that it should be made mandatory for the Railway
 Administration not to reject or overrule any recommendations made by the Commissioners without a meeting between
 the Chairman, Railway Board and the Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety, where the matters can be discussed
 threadbare and agreements reached.  The Committee further recommends that while expressing their inability to accept
 the recommendations, the Railway Board should give detailed reasons for not accepting the recommendations.  The
 Committee also recommends that any decision taken by the Railway Board in consultation with the Commission of
 Railway Safety must not be revoked unilaterally by the Railway Board or Zonal Railway, without prior consultation
 and approval of the Commission.
(Para 27)
 
The Committee observes that a large number of new passenger trains are introduced every year to meet the demand of
 the traveling public.  While it does fulfil the requirements of the public, it has to be examined as to whether such an
 action is in the interest of safety and convenience of the traveling public.  The present system in the country is already
 overstressed and it is important to ensure that all infrastructure facilities cater to the safe running of additional trains
 with due safety margins.  It is essential that such facilities are in position before adding any burden of additional trains. 
 The introduction of additional trains involves the safety of the passengers.   The Committee is not convinced with the
 reply furnished by the Ministry of Railways with regard to not seeking the concurrence of Commission of Railway
 Safety before introduction of a new passenger train.  The Committee gives due weightage to the reply of the Ministry of
 Railways that before any new train is introduced, certification of available maintenance infrastructure at either end is
 given by two SAG (Joint Secretaries) Officers, in-charge of operation and maintenance, after consulting all concerned
 agencies.  Ministry of Railway have also pointed out that concurrence of every new train does not fall under the legal
 duties of Commission of Railway Safety, as enumerated in the Railway Act, 1989.  The main task of the Commission is
 to direct, advise and caution the railway executives through its regulation/inspectional/audit and investigatory/advisory
 functions and thereby assist them in ensuring that all stipulated measures are taken in regard to the soundness of rail
 construction and safety in train operation.   The Committee is, therefore, of the view that the sanction of Commission of
 Railway Safety must be necessary for Ministry of Railways before introducing any new passenger train.  The
 Committee, therefore, recommends that it should be made mandatory for Ministry of Railways to seek the concurrence

R E P O R T
In June 2001, the erstwhile Ministry of Surface Transport was bifurcated into two Ministries viz. Ministry of

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/84threport.htm[28-08-2018 13:07:32]
 Road Transport & Highways and Ministry of Shipping.  These two Ministries have been reconstituted into one Ministry,
 viz. Ministry of Shipping, Road Transport and Highways in September 2004 with two Departments i.e. Department of
 Road Transport and Highways and Department of Shipping.
 2.         The Department of Road Transport and Highways is responsible for the formulation and implementation of
 policies relating to Road Transport and National Highways, Central Sector Road Schemes, administration of Central
 Road Fund and sponsoring of research pertaining to road works.  The two major divisions of the Department are the
 Transport Division and the Road Division.
 
3.         The Road Transport Division of the Department is concerned with the formulation of broad policies related to
 road transport besides, making arrangements for the movement of vehicular traffic with the neighboring countries. 
 
4.         The Road Division is concerned mainly with matters relating to:-
(i)                    Advising Government on all general policy matters relating to Highways
(ii)                  Development and maintenance of roads declared as National Highways
(iii)                 Development and maintenance of roads other than National Highways in   Union Territories.
(iv)                Administration of Central Road Fund (CRF) pertaining to state roads other than rural roads.
(v)                  Evaluation and specification of Standards for roads and bridges
(vi)        Research on roads. 
 5.         The following autonomous bodies function under the administrative control of the Department of Road
 Transport and Highways:-
(a)                National Highways Authority of India
(b)               National Institute of Training of Highway Engineers (NITHE).
 
6.         Demand No.86 containing the details of budget allocation of the Department of Road Transport and Highways
 for the financial year 2005-06 was considered by the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
 Transport, Tourism and Culture at its meeting held on the 31
st March 2005.  During the meeting, the Committee took
 oral evidence of the Secretary and other officers of the Department of Road Transport and Highways.

10.       The Committee had in its 82 nd Report on Demands for Grants 2004-05 of the Ministry of Road Transport and

 Plan and had, therefore, recommended that the budgetary allocations of the Ministry should be substantially increased at
 RE stage.  Also the allocations of the Ministry should be adequately increased during the remaining years of Tenth Plan
 so as to reduce the resource gap in this sector to some extent.  In their Action Taken Replies furnished to the Committee,
 the Department of Road Transport and Highways replied that the suggestion of the Committee has been noted for
 compliance and Planning Commission shall be approached for allocations during the remaining years of the Tenth Plan. 
 As desired by the Committee, the budget allocation for the road sector has been projected as Rs.13948.32 crore in RE
 2004-05 as against the budget provision of Rs.10770 crore.
 
11.       However, from a perusal of the Demands for Grants 2005-06 of the Department of Road Transport and
 Highways, the Committee observed that the BE 2004-05 of the Department was reduced from Rs.9637 crore to Rs.8566
 crore at RE stage.  The Committee asked the Department of Road Transport and Highways about the reasons that the
 budget provisions of the Department were reduced at RE stage inspite of its increased projection by the Department.
 
12.       In response, the Department of Road Transport and Highways explained to the Committee that the Budget
 Estimate for 2004-2005 for the Department including the provision for Road Transport was Rs.7912 crore as ‘Plan’
 provision and Rs.1725 crore as ‘Non Plan’ provision.  In addition to the ‘Plan’ provision, there was an IEBR component
 of Rs.3300 crore making a total Plan provision of Rs.11,212 crore.  At the RE stage, the plan provisions were brought
 down from Rs.7912 crore to 6766 crore and IEBR of Rs.3300 crore to ‘Nil’ and accordingly indicating total of Rs.6766
 crore.  The Non Plan provision was enhanced from Rs.1725 crore to Rs.1800 crore.  The plan provisions came down on
 account of slow implementation of Externally Aided projects by NHAI and the Department.  The Externally Aided
 component of NHAI came down from Rs.3210 crore to Rs.2000 crore and the provision for the Department for
 Externally Aided Project came down from Rs.113.50 crore to Rs.30 crore.  However, there was an increase of the outlay
 under NH (O) of Rs.147.5 crore which was provided out of the surrenders made on account of the Externally Aided
 Projects (EAP).   The reasons for the reduced demand for the EAP have been explained below.
 
13.       The Ministry had projected a requirement of Rs.13,948.32 crore (only for the ‘Road’ sector) at the RE stage on
 account of :
(i)                             Allotment of additional cess of Rs.0.50 per litre of diesel and petrol which was accruing
 w.e.f. 1
st April, 2003.
(ii)                            An additional demand for capital works under NH(O) Plan and for National Highways
 entrusted to the BRO and also for the strategic roads being implemented by the BRO.
(iii)                          Reduced demand for the Externally Aided Project.
 
14.       The BE 2004-05 of the Department was Rs.7912 crore which includes Rs.44 crore for the Road Transport Sector,
 leaving a balance of Rs.7868 crore for the Road Sector.  The provision becomes Rs.10,770 crore at BE stage after
 including Rs.2812 crores as Inter Account Transfer from the CRF and Rs.90 crore from the Permanent Bridge Fee Fund.

20.       The Committee regrets to note that BE Plan Provision of Rs.7912 crore of Department of Road Transport and
 Highways was brought down to Rs.6766 crore on account of slow implementation of Externally Aided Projects by
 NHAI and the Department.  Further, there was delay in finalisation of the loans and obtaining approvals for the
 procurement for the externally aided component of the Corridor Project of NHDP (Phase-II) being financed by the
 Asian Development Bank (ADB).  Also, there was delay in award of works to the contractors and consultants for
 development of NH-34 in West Bengal.  These instances clearly bring out that on the one hand, the Department of Road
 Transport and Highways emphasizes that funds for development and maintenance of National Highways are inadequate
 while, on the other hand, the Department is not able to utilise the higher allocation made to it at BE stage.   The
 Department has failed to make optimal utilization of the funds at its disposal. The reasons for shortfall mentioned are
 delay in land acquisition, poor performance of the contractors, law and order problem etc. are very general in nature and
 are repeated every year. As a result of these, the budgetary allocations of the Department were reduced at RE stage.  The
 Committee is of the view that there is a lack of monitoring system in the Department of Road Transport and Highways. 
 The lack of a proper monitoring system in the Department is exemplified by the delay and non-completion of the
 construction of flyover at Murthal in Haryana and the failure of the Department of Road Transport and Highways in
 verifying the credentials of the contractors who had submitted forged bank guarantees.  The Committee observes that
 the budget allocations of the Department of Road Transport and Highways have been substantially increased during
 2005-06. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Road Transport and Highways should devise
 strategies, whereby they are able to fully utilize the funds at their disposal.  They should also evolve some mechanism to
 identify bottlenecks causing delays and work towards resolving all such hindrances in coordination with all the
 concerned agencies.  This would also help them to avoid time overrun and consequential cost overrun of the projects to
 be executed by them.
 
NATIONAL HIGHWAYS
21.       India has a vast road network of 3.32 million kilometers of which the National Highways and the State Highways
 together account for 1,95,000 km.  As on 31
st March 2004, the length of National Highways network is only 65,569 km
 constituting about 2% of the total road network in the country and carrying about 40% of the total traffic across the
 length and breadth of the country.
 
22.       The Department of Road Transport & Highways is primarily responsible for the construction and maintenance of
 National Highways (NH). All roads, other than National Highway in States, fall within the jurisdiction of respective
 state governments.  The development and maintenance of National Highways are being done on agency basis.  The
 National Highways Authority of India (NHAI), State Public Works Departments (PWDs) and the Border Road
 Organisation (BRO) are the main agencies. Out of the total National Highway length of 65,569 km, about 14,279 km
 have been entrusted to National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) for improvement under National Highway
 Development Project (NHDP) Phase I & II, Port Connectivity Schemes and other schemes.  The balance lengths of
 about 46,586 km and 4,704 km of non-NHDP sections of National Highways are mainly entrusted to State PWDs and
 Border Roads Organisation (BRO) respectively, as agencies of the Ministry. 
 
NATIONAL HIGHWAYS DEVELOPMENT PROJECT (NHDP)
23.       The Ministry of Road Transport & Highways informed the Committee that the Government has embarked upon a
 massive programme to develop highways through the National Highways Development Project (NHDP) in the country. 
 The NHDP is the largest highway project ever undertaken in the country.  This is being implemented by National
 Highways Authority of India.  The NHDP consists of Golden Quadrilateral, North-South and East-West Corridors, Port
 Connectivity and other Projects.  The total length under NHDP is about 14,279 km.  The details relating to NHDP are as
 under:-
(i)                  Golden Quadrilateral (GQ) comprising National Highways connecting four metro cities viz., Delhi,
 Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata.  Total length of GQ is 5846 km.  As on 28
th February 2005, four-laning of

CENTRAL ROAD FUND
36.       Funds for development and maintenance of National Highways are provided by the Central Government on
 yearly basis. Budgetary allocation, however, had fallen short of the requirements. In recognition of the need for funds
 for the road sector, the Union Budget for 1998-99 provided for a levy of additional excise duty and additional customs
 duty of Re.1.00 per litre of petrol. Accruals from this were made available to the National Highways Authority of India
 in 1998-99. Subsequently, an additional duty of Re.1.00 per litre on imported and domestic high speed diesel oil was
 levied from 1999-2000. In 2003-04, an additional cess of 50 paise per litre was levied on petrol and diesel. In Finance
 Minister’s budget speech for 2005-06, additional cess of 50 paise has been proposed exclusively for National
 Highways.  Revenues from these two levies are to accrue to a dedicated Central Road Fund.  This fund is a non-lapsable
 fund.  The fund has been given statutory status by the Central Road Fund Act, 2000. 
 
37.       Allocation from the Central Road Fund are being made in the following manner:-
(i)                  50 per cent of the cess on high-speed diesel oil for development of rural roads.
 
(ii)                50 per cent of cess of High Speed Diesel (HSD) and the entire cess collected on petrol are being
 allocated as per the following:-
 
(a)                An amount equal to 57.5 per cent of such sum for the development and maintenance of
 National Highways;
(b)               The amount equal to 12.5 per cent for the construction of road under or over bridges and
 safety works at unmanned railway crossings; and
(c)                An amount equal to 30 per cent on development and maintenance of State roads.  Out of this
 amount, 10 per cent i.e., 3 per cent of the total share of the State Roads shall be kept as reserved
 by the Central Government for allocation to States for implementation of State Road Schemes of
 Inter-State and economic importance to be approved by the Central Government.

40.       The Committee had noted that although an additional levy of cess of 50 paise per litre was being levied on petrol
 and diesel w.e.f. 1.4.2003, the funds were not being transferred to the Department of Road Transport and Highways.

 grant.
 
(b)          The Finance Ministry may allocate an additional sum every year to the Ministry of Shipping, Road
 Transport & Highways (Department of Road Transport & Highways) for being passed on to the National
 Highways Authority of India over and above the annual budgetary allocations, on the same principle to
 cover the shortfall of National Highways at the existing apportionment formula and the proposed
 apportionment formula, so that National Highways Authority of India can suitably leverage assured
 inflow of funds.
 
(c)           Finance Ministry may immediately release the share of National Highways from the accruals already
 received from additional cess from 1.4.2003 as per the existing formula under Central Road Fund Act,

64.       During the meeting of the Committee held on 31

 of Road Transport and Highways the need to have an integrated transport policy in the country.  The Committee pointed
 out the availability of various types of transport systems in the country and that passenger traffic was not
 proportionately distributed.  The Committee sought the opinion of the representatives of Department of Road Transport
 and Highways in the matter.  In response, while agreeing to the need to have an integrated transport policy, the
 Secretary of the Department stated as under:-

 with roads; the Shipping deals with shipping; the Civil Aviation deals with it.  One has to see it either the
 Planning Commission can do it or we can come up with an integrated transport policy for the road sector.   But,
 we are in touch with the Planning Commission on this issue.  Whatever decision is taken by the Government as a
 whole, we will abide by that.”
 65.       The Committee observes that one of the objectives for the Tenth Plan for the road sector is ‘Development of
 roads to be considered an integral part of the total transport system supplementing other modes, integrating the
 development plans with railways and other modes of transport’.   This objective of the Tenth Plan reinforces the need to
 have an integrated transport policy in the country.  The Committee is of the view that the modal-mix in terms of
 transport is very adverse in the country inspite of the fact that we have long inland waterways, a fairly large railway
 network and the recent upsurge in the aviation and road transport sector.  However, in absence of the right kind of
 modal-mix the country is not making optimum utilization of all those resources.  There is, therefore, a need to have a
 more balanced and equitable distribution of passenger and freight traffic in the country.  The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that the Government must come forward with an integrated transport policy to make optimum utilization
 of the various transport facilities available in the country.

DAMAGE IN TSUMANI HIT AREAS
66.       The Tsunami waves hit the coastal regions of the country in December 2004 and caused a major loss of life and
 property there. The Committee desired to know from the Department of Road Transport and Highways about the
 damage caused to the road network and the relief measures undertaken by the Department in the southern parts of the
 country and Andaman & Nicobar Islands. In response, the Department of Road Transport and Highways informed the
 Committee that the Tsumani waves that hit the coastal regions of south India in December 2004 caused huge loss of life
 and property and extensive damage to road network and bridges.  Five teams of officers from the Department inspected
 the affected areas to assess the damages to road infrastructure.  About 242 km of National Highways and 520 km of
 state roads, 14 bridges and 78 culverts have been damaged in the states of Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and
 Union Territories of Andaman & Nicobar Islands and Pondicherry.   The total cost of repairs to damaged National
 Highways and state roads has been assessed at about Rs.200 crore (Rs.31.5 crore for short term and Rs.168.5 crore for
 long term measures).  The following relief measures were undertaken by the Department:-
A Control Room was set up by the Department which functioned from         28 th December 2004 to 28th January
 2005.  It was done with the help of all the concerned field agencies as well as other Ministries.
 
The Arasalar Bridge on NH-45A near Karaikal in the Union Territory of Pondicherry was damaged. A bailey
 bridge has been provided for immediate restoration of traffic.  A bridge by the side of the existing bridge is to be
 constructed as a permanent measure.
 
There have been extensive damages to the road network and bridges in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands also. 
 The Andaman and Nicobar Public Works Department (PWD) had requested for the supply of six power saws,
 eight generators, 20 water pumps, 6000 metre G.I. Pipes, 10 plate compactors, 100 metric tonne cement, 100
 pieces RCC Hume Pipes, 10 hand rammers, 500 metre flexible hose, 1000 metre ERW steel pipes, etc. for
 restoration works.  These items were sent by air/ship.
 
67.       The Committee was further informed that the superstructure of a 160 metre  long bridge over the Pazhyar river in
 Tamil Nadu was washed away by the tsunami waves.  The Department of Road Transport and Highways provided relief
 measures by operationalising a ferry service pending installation of a temporary steel bridge and installing a temporary
 steel bridge within 6 weeks for immediate restoration of traffic.  In addition, a permanent bridge was also proposed to be
 constructed within one and a half years.
 
68.       The Department further stated that 23 proposals amounting to Rs.80 crore had been received from the states of
 Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Union Territories of Pondicherry for restoration of the above damages.  All
 these proposals are still under examination.
 
69.       The Committee observes that the Tsunami waves caused extensive damage to the road network and bridges in the
 Southern Parts of the country.  The Committee appreciates the promptness with which the Department of Road
 Transport and Highways responded to the situation and carried out the relief measures in the tsunami hit areas.  The
 Committee strongly recommends that the Department should consider the proposals submitted by the State
 Governments for restoration of the damages on priority basis so that construction/repair works could be carried out at
 the earliest.  The Committee further observes that damage to the National Highways has badly affected the tourism
 potential in the Andaman & Nicobar Islands, which is the lifeline of these islands.  The Committee recommends that
 priority should be given to the restoration of the National Highway network and bridges etc. in these islands.

 important steps taken by them to control vehicular pollution which are as under:-
·        From 1.4.2000, unleaded petrol has been made available in the country.
·        Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) and Liquified Petroleum Gas (LPG) have been  permitted to be used as
 alternate auto fuels.
·        India 2000 (India stage I) which are akin to Euro I norms have been made effective from 1.4.2000 throughout
 the country.
·        Bharat Stage II emission norms  which are akin to Euro II norms have already been introduced in the eleven
 mega cities and are envisaged to come into force all over India from 1.4.2005. 
·        Bharat Stage III emission standards which are akin to Euro III norms, have been notified  to come into force in
 11 mega cities from 1.4.2005.
·        The emission norms for tractors were first notified in the year 1999 and the next stage emission norms  for
 these vehicles have also come into force from 1.6.2003.  Further, even tighter emission norms for new tractors 
 are coming into force w.e.f. 1.10.2005.
·        Stricter Pollution Under Control norms have been introduced for on-road motor vehicles from 1.10.2004. 
 Apart from tighter norms for Carbon Mono Oxide (CO), the measurement of Hydro Carbon (HC) in respect of
 petrol driven vehicles have also been introduced.  Further, the testing protocol in respect of diesel vehicles has
 also been defined. States have also been empowered to prescribe tighter norms in specific areas, if there is such
 a need and the infrastructure available enables doing so.

 various States/UTs.

 mentions that workshop-cum-training programmes are organized every year at the Automotive Research Association of
 India (ARAI), Pune where officers of State Transport Departments are trained in matters of transport management and
 environmental issues.  During the evidence of the Secretary of Department of Road Transport & Highways held on 31
st
 March 2005, the Committee brought to his notice that no details pertaining to Automotive Research Association of India
 were available in the documents furnished by the Department.  The Committee also pointed out that there were

 irregularities in the functioning of the above organisation.  In response, the Secretary of the Department merely stated
 that the Automotive Research Association of India was not under their Ministry and that it was under the Ministry of

95.       The Committee understands that Automotive Research Association of India, Pune has been set up by the Indian
 vehicle and automotive ancillary manufacturers and it is the Department of Road Transport & Highways's authorised
 certification agency for emissions norms etc.  Almost all vehicle manufacturers and major ancillary manufacturers are
 members of this institute.  The Committee is at a loss to understand as to why Government of India's emission norms
 etc. may be certified by an agency which has vehicle manufacturers as its members and on which the Department of
 Road Transport & Highways does not have any administrative control.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that
 either the Department of Road Transport & Highways should have control on the Automotive Research Association of
 India, Pune or the Association should be divested of the power of fixing emission norms as apex certification agency.  It
 is a direct case of the manufacturers themselves being the regulators, which promotes the scope of corruption in the
 functioning of the Institute.  The Committee desires that a proper enquiry may be instituted in the functioning of this
 institute.

 Rs.7.00 lakh for Research & Development out of the total allocation of Rs.7.9 crore during 2004-05, which makes
 evident as to how much priority the Department of Road Transport & Highways attaches to the Research &
 Development activities.  The Committee is dissatisfied that the Department of Road Transport & Highways has no
 Research & Development mechanism of its own and the Department has to depend upon other organisations for its
 Research & Development activities.  The Committee recommends that Department of Road Transport and Highways
 should develop an institutional mechanism to undertake research and development activities.  The Department should
 also create a regulator of its own with the requisite technical wherewithal for fixing emission norms, product design and
 development etc.  The Committee also recommends that the Research & Development activities should also be used for
 developing technology for creating cost-effective high quality road network such as existing in Malaysia and some other
 countries.
97.       The Committee observes that development of road data bank and computerized project monitoring system and
 promotion of use of information technology in the highway sector is one of the objectives of the Government in the
 Tenth Plan.  However, it appears that the Government has not achieved much progress in this sector especially the use
 of Information Technology in online  project monitoring system.  The Committee is of the view that Information
 Technology can also be used as an effective tool for monitoring the implementation of the projects undertaken by the
 Department.    They should also make efforts to integrate research and development activities with their monitoring
 system so that proper monitoring could be kept on the projects undertaken by them, which will also help them to keep
 tab on time overrun and cost overrun of such projects.   The Committee also recommends that efforts cited by the
 Department of Road Transport & Highways like creation of Ministry's chair in the area of development of highway
 system at Indian Institutes of Technology and creation of independent testing facilities for bridges on National
 Highways at Central Road Research Institute, New Delhi may be pursued more vigorously and in case of any difficulty,
 parallel institutions may be identified for Research & Development activities.

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
 
ANALYSIS OF THE TENTH PLAN PROVISIONS AND ANNUAL PLAN   2005-06
            The Committee regrets to note that BE Plan Provision of Rs.7912 crore of Department of Road Transport and
 Highways was brought down to Rs.6766 crore on account of slow implementation of Externally Aided Projects by
 NHAI and the Department.  Further, there was delay in finalisation of the loans and obtaining approvals for the
 procurement for the externally aided component of the Corridor Project of NHDP (Phase-II) being financed by the
 Asian Development Bank (ADB).  Also, there was delay in award of works to the contractors and consultants for
 development of NH-34 in West Bengal.  These instances clearly bring out that on the one hand, the Department of Road
 Transport and Highways emphasizes that funds for development and maintenance of National Highways are inadequate
 while, on the other hand, the Department is not able to utilise the higher allocation made to it at BE stage.   The
 Department has failed to make optimal utilization of the funds at its disposal. The reasons for shortfall mentioned are
 delay in land acquisition, poor performance of the contractors, law and order problem etc. are very general in nature and
 are repeated every year. As a result of these, the budgetary allocations of the Department were reduced at RE stage.  The
 Committee is of the view that there is a lack of monitoring system in the Department of Road Transport and Highways.

NATIONAL HIGHWAYS DEVELOPMENT PROJECT (NHDP)
            The Committee notes that the target date of completion of the Golden Quadrilateral has been revised twice i.e.
 from December 2003 to December 2004 and now upto December 2005.  The Committee had discussed this issue in its
 82
nd Report on Demands for Grants 2004-05 of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways and recommended that
 the Government should take all necessary steps to make sure that the works proposed to be completed by December
 2004 are completed within that period.  However, the Committee notes that the progress of four-laning on the Golden
 Quadrilateral project as on December 2004 was only 74%.  Thus, the steps taken by Department of Road Transport and
 Highways for timely completion of the project had not been adequate.  The Committee, therefore, would like to reiterate
 its earlier recommendation made in its 82 nd Report that the Government should take all necessary steps and evolve a
 monitoring mechanism to ensure quality of construction, making officials accountable for failure, transparency in
 implementation process, penalizing defaulting contractors etc. so that the remaining part of the project is completed by
 December 2005 and the need to further revise the target date of completion does not arise.
(Para 29)
NATIONAL HIGHWAYS NOT COVERED UNDER NHDP
            The Committee notes that in response to its recommendation for an equitable development of non-NHDP
 National Highways, the Department of Road Transport and Highways has formulated projects for development of such
 highways.  The Committee recommends that the Government should give its approval for the Accelerated North-East
 Road Development Project and NHDP Phase IV at the earliest.  Also the projects under NHDP Phase III should be
 taken up at the earliest so that the deadlines set for these projects are met.  The Committee is of the view that
 Department of Road Transport and Highways has now gained sufficient experience during the implementation of
 Golden Quadrilateral.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that Department of Road Transport and Highways
 should adopt a proactive approach and take care that the hindrances resulting in delay in timely completion of such
 projects do not recur.  Action should be taken in advance to ensure that such bottlenecks do not impede the timely
 implementation of the projects and the deadlines set for the project are met unlike the Golden Quadrilateral where the
 target date of completion has gone up by two years so far.  
                                                                                                                            
                                                                                (Para 35)
CENTRAL ROAD FUND
            The Committee takes exception to the fact that funds accruing to the Central Road Fund due to levy of additional
 cess since 1.4.2003 have not been provided to the Department of Road Transport and Highways, inspite of the fact that
 this additional cess of 50 paise per litre on petrol and diesel was levied primarily to support the implementation of
 National Highway Development Project (NHDP).  There has been no positive outcome to this impasse inspite of a
 direction by the Cabinet for implementation of the recommendations of the Group of Ministers.  The Committee
 recommends that the Department of Road Transport and Highways should take up the matter with the Ministry of
 Finance  so that the funds due to the Department are provided to it at the earliest and the projects under National
 Highway Development Project do not suffer for want of funds.

DEVELOPMENT OF NATIONAL HIGHWAYS IN NORTH-EASTERN REGION
            One of the objectives of the Tenth Plan for Road Sector is special attention to the development of roads in North-
Eastern region.  Although three years of the Five Year Plan have gone by, the Government has not taken any concrete
 steps for improving the National Highways network in this region.  Also, the Special Accelerated Road Development
 Programme in the North-Eastern region is still under consideration of the Government. The Committee feels that
 development of road network is very crucial in the context of the development of North-Eastern region of the country.

 HIGHWAYS
            The Committee feels that in view of the huge resource gap of around Rs.1,06,000 crore in the road sector during
 the Tenth Plan, there is a genuine need to attract private sector investment in this sector to a large extent.  However, the
 Government has not been able to attract private sector investment to the desired extent.  The Committee recommends
 that the Government should project the success of the Golden Quadrilateral to the private sector to encourage them to
 contribute more and more to the development of this sector.  This would definitely help the Government to reduce the
 resource gap position to a large extent.
            The Committee is apprehensive whether the Government will be able to ensure private sector participation in the
 North-Eastern region of the country to the extent required by them.  The Committee recommends that, in such a
 scenario, keeping in view the socio-economic conditions of the North-Eastern region, the Government must provide
 resources for the projects on its own and the developmental activities in road sector for North-Eastern region should not
 be allowed to be a casualty.

NEED FOR AN INTEGRATED TRANSPORT POLICY
            The Committee observes that one of the objectives for the Tenth Plan for the road sector is ‘Development of
 roads to be considered an integral part of the total transport system supplementing other modes, integrating the
 development plans with railways and other modes of transport’.   This objective of the Tenth Plan reinforces the need to
 have an integrated transport policy in the country.  The Committee is of the view that the modal-mix in terms of
 transport is very adverse in the country inspite of the fact that we have long inland waterways, a fairly large railway
 network and the recent upsurge in the aviation and road transport sector.  However, in absence of the right kind of
 modal-mix the country is not making optimum utilization of all those resources.  There is, therefore, a need to have a
 more balanced and equitable distribution of passenger and freight traffic in the country.  The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that the Government must come forward with an integrated transport policy to make optimum utilization
 of the various transport facilities available in the country.

 culture is the most crucial role-player which gives meaning to our present existence. The role of Culture lies not only in the context of promotion of economic growth but also in relation to
 other objectives of creating an environment that encourages self-expression and exploration on the part of individuals and communities besides support to arts and artists and encouraging

2.         The Ministry of Culture, which was set up in 1985 through the 174 th Amendment of the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961 was part of the Ministry of
 Human Resource Development; later it was transferred to the newly created Ministry of Tourism and Culture. In May 2004 it has been declared as an independent Ministry and is now
 Ministry of Culture. The Ministry is responsible for the promotion, preservation and conservation of the tangible and intangible cultural heritage of the country. It also promotes mutual
 understanding, goodwill and foster closer relations with foreign countries. Preservation of ancient and historic monuments and records, exploration and excavation of archaeological sites
 and remains, maintenance and expansion of libraries and museums of national importance and observance of centenaries and anniversaries of eminent personalities are among its other
 responsibilities. The institutions of the Ministry, which are engaged in promotion, and dissemination of art and culture broadly are the Zonal  Cultural Centers, Center for Cultural Resources
 and Training, and through the Schemes operated Departmentally. The public private participation in the Ministry is done under the aegis of the National Culture Fund.
3.         The programmes undertaken by the Ministry of Culture can broadly be classified as, Activities of North East Region, Archaeology, Museums, Anthropology and Ethnology,
 Archives and Archival Libraries, Tibetan/Buddhist Studies, Libraries, Akademies and National School of Drama, Promotion and Dissemination of Culture, Memorials, Centenaries and
 Anniversaries, Cultural Relations and Festival of India, IGNCA and Secretariat.
4.         Plan programmes of the Ministry of Culture relating to promotion, preservation and conservation of the cultural heritage of the country is implemented through a network of 2
 attached offices, 6 subordinate offices and 26 Autonomous organisations under its control and through 16 schemes directly operated by the Ministry for promotion and dissemination of art
 and culture.  Its activities and programmes have been organized under eleven broad heads. They are Promotion & Dissemination, Archaeology, Museums, Archives, Anthropology,
 Performing Arts, Libraries, Buddhist and Tibetan Institutes, Activities for North Eastern Region and Other Expenditure.

8.         Demand No.20 containing the details of budget allocation of the Ministry of Culture for the financial year 2005-06 was considered by the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
 Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture at its meeting held on the 29
th March 2005.  The Secretary Ministry of Culture during the course of oral evidence held on 29 th March 2005,
 deposed before the Committee :
“This year has been a difficult year for them as the Ministry had major financial constraints.  The budget was passed late and they had accordingly a shorter time to spend the
 money allocated to them.  There was also a cap by the Ministry of Finance.   Accordingly the Ministry of Culture had to spend 65% of the money by December and thereafter
 there was a slash of about Rs.65 crore at the revised budget stage.  After intervention of the Ministry they got restoration of the cut to the extent of Rs.20 crore.  But this has
 certainly put a strain on the institutions/field offices functioning under the Ministry.”
 
9.         The Committee is happy to note that the Ministry of Culture had proposed an outlay of Rs.551.12 crore and also got an approved outlay of the same amount with a capital component
 of Rs.61.80 crore.   The Committee hopes that the Ministry of Culture will be able to utilize the funds for implementation of new Schemes/Projects optimally. 
10.       The Committee, however, is not convinced about the reasons cited by the Ministry that budget was passed late and accordingly, there was shorter time available to spend the money
 allocated to them and observes that if the annual plan starts after the beginning of the financial year itself, then it considerably reduces the capacity of the Ministry to plan out expenditure.  
 Therefore, the planning for financial progress has to start even before as the broad heads are already known to the Ministry under the contours of the five-year plan.  The Committee also
 fails to understand as to how this intra-year financial development should deter the Ministry in planning it in such a manner that none of the financial allocations made can be successfully
 used by the end of the year.  Therefore, the Committee strongly recommends that the Finance Ministry recalling the money which has been already allocated is a serious problem and the
 Ministry should take adequate care and evolve a sound method of financial planning so that such kind of circumstance may never occur in future.

ARCHAEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA
 14.      The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) was established in 1861.  It is an attached office of the Ministry of Culture.  Since its establishment, 144 years ago, the ASI has grown into
 a large organization having its network throughout the country.  At present, the ASI has declared 3656 monuments, which are of national importance in the country, including 17 properties
 inscribed on the World Heritage List by UNESCO.  The major activities of the ASI are maintenance, conservation and preservation of centrally protected monuments/sites and remains.  It
 conducts archeological exploration and excavation regularly.  It also keeps developing epigraphical research, setting up and reorganization of site museums and training in archaeology. The
 Archaeological Survey of India has prepared perspective plans for the 10
th Five Year Plan period which envisaged an integrated approach covering conservation, preservation, landscaping,
 organizing/ re-organising of site museums and problem oriented excavations and exploration.   With a holistic approach, the Archaeological Survey of India is devoted towards creation of
 cultural hubs encompassing facilities for domestic and foreign tourists.  The proposed cultural hubs are, i.e. Mahabalipuram, Ajanta & Ellora , Hampi, Kurukshetra, Chittorgarh,
 Kumbhalgarh, Sibsagar monuments and   Fatehpur Sikri.

 during the year 2004-05 was Rs.70.00 Crores.  Subsequently Ministry of Culture has reduced the Plan budget allocation to Archaeological Survey of India for 2004-05 to Rs.48.00 Crores.

 into consideration the above, the Ministry of Culture partially restored the budget allocation (Plan), under R.E. for 2004-05 to Rs.58.00 Crores.  Ministry of Culture has conveyed that

18.       The Committee notes that the Plan Allocation for ASI has been increased by Rs.10.00 crore in BE 2005-06.  The Committee hopes that this increased allocation would be utilized on

(i)         Non-Writing/Publication of Excavation Reports
19.       In the absence of timely publication of reports, achievements of ASI remains largely unattended and unnoticed by the public. Therefore the Committee enquired about the
 outstanding delay in publication/non-writing of Excavation Report. In their replied the Ministry of Culture informed the Committee that a Steering Committee was formed by the DG, ASI
 to look into the question of pending excavation reports.  The Steering Committee has identified 56 pending excavation reports out of which 17 are pertaining to large-scale excavations and
 39 to small-scale excavations.  The Committee laid down a time frame of 6 months for submission of reports of small-scale excavations and 15 months for large-scale excavations. 
 However, 32 reports are to be written by the retired officers and most of them have expressed their inability to write the reports or asked for several facilities for completing them.  Hence, it
 has been decided to assign this task to the serving officers who were earlier associated with the excavations.  A time frame of 24 months is considered to be reasonable for completion of the
 excavation reports. The Ministry also informed that the Archeological Survey of India has communicated to all the excavators both in service and the retired, requesting them to complete
 them pending excavation report within stipulated time-frame.  The Ministry further informed that some of the excavators have positively responded to this.
20.       The Committee in its 80
th Report on the Demands for Grants (2004-05) had recommended that the Ministry should not only take initiative in publishing reports in time but also to
 digitize the reports as a result of which those can be preserved for longer period.  The Ministry of Culture in the Action Taken Replies to this recommendation had observed that
 "Digitization of various archeological reports may be taken up after observing the required codal formalities".  The Committee again further enquired that as to how long the Ministry would
 take to implement this and fulfill the required codal formalities.  At this stage, the Ministry informed that ASI has not yet taken up any programme of digitization of archaeological reports. 
21.       The Committee is of the opinion that if the excavation reports are not published in time then all the tax payers money spent on them goes waste.  The Committee is utterly dissatisfied
 that despite repeated recommendations made earlier by this Committee, the Ministry is still not in a position to indicate specific time frame by when this job will be accomplished.  The
 Committee observes that the labour and the money gone into excavations undertaken by the Archaeological Survey of India for the knowledge to crystallize for generations and the efforts
 to make excavations more understandable becomes fruitful only when the findings are documented.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that all excavation reports should be published
 within a specific time frame in order to check this massive national loss. 
22.       The Committee feels that the Ministry of Culture has taken the recommendation of the Standing Committee contained in its 80
th Report on the Demands for Grants (2004-2005)
 regarding digitization of Archaeological Reports in a casual manner and till now has not been able to firm up its view in the matter.   Therefore, the Ministry may consider the
 recommendation of the Committee and take up the programme of digitization of  Archeological Reports. 
 
(ii)        Merger of National Mission on Antiquities and National Mission on Built Heritage:
 
23.       The Ministry of Culture had launched two Missions namely, National Mission on Antiquities and National Mission on Built Heritage, with following major objectives:-
·        To create widespread awareness about the antiquities and built heritage and the laws governing it.
·        Creation of a credible National Data Bank of Built Heritage and Antiquities.
·        Selected monuments from different parts of the country will be taken up for structural conservation.
·        Out reach programmes will be organized to create public awareness of our rich cultural heritage and the ways by which it can be sustained.  Besides attempt will be made to create
 synergy amongst various institutions and organisations working towards a similar goal.
·        Mission would help in capacity building in heritage care in State Archaeology, Museums and NGOs.
·        Mission would help the concerned authorities in the formulation of national, state and local policy in safeguarding and management of heritage.

 no time overrun beyond the five years period prescribed for the Project.  The Mission would be able to generate public awareness and synergy between Archaeological Survey of
 India  and several other institutions working in the field.  The two Missions proposals on Built Heritage and Antiquities have been merged.  Initially two documents for two Missions
 i.e. Antiquities and Built heritage were prepared with Archaeological Survey of India  as the Nodal Agency.  As the objectives of both the Missions were overlapping and Mission
 structure had been streamlined, it was felt that a single Mission structure for both the Missions i.e. for Built Heritage and Antiquities could undertake the work.  Moreover the
 expertise required for undertaking the work of both the Missions is similar; hence twin Mission proposal has been recast into a single Mission proposal.  By merging them together,
 the financial outlay required for undertaking both the Missions has been greatly reduced and the goals are also justified.”
 
25.       The Director-General, Archeological Survey of India during the course of oral evidence submitted before the Committee that :
 
"… there is a shortage of staff in the ASI mostly on the conservation side.  We do not have conservation professionals in various disciplines.  So far as the mission is
 concerned, we will be engaging people on short-term basis.  Because the essential job is documentation."
 
 
26.       In view of the explanation given by the Ministry the Committee concludes that the whole process indicates confusion in the decision making process and complete lack of
 farsightedness on the part of the Ministry in planning its programmes and projects which has not only affected the rich cultural heritage of the country but also led to valuable wastage of
 time and resources. 
27.       The Committee fails to understand that why so much additional work was given to the ASI when ASI was not able to successfully complete the work already assigned.  The
 Committee is also not convinced about the objectives of these Mission modes.  On the one hand the Ministry has stated that they are not recruiting more staff.  On the other hand the
 Committee has been informed that for the Mission purpose the Ministry will be contractualising jobs on short term basis.  In view of this the Committee directs that the Ministry should
 adopt a clear cut guideline in this regard and the ASI should be provided with appropriate wherewithal so that laudable goals of these Missions do not remain unachieved.
 
(iii)       Problem of Encroachment and Security of Monuments/Sites under the Protection of ASI:
 
28.       The Committee was quite concerned about the illegal encroachment of monuments/sites under the protection of ASI and desired to know from the Ministry as to what was being done
 to check the encroachment around the monuments.  The Ministry of Culture replied that as and when an encroachment is noticed in the protected area of a monument, the Superintending
 Archaeologist issues a notice to the encroacher as per the provisions of the Ancient  Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958.  A complaint is also lodged with the local
 police.  When no response is received from the encroacher, the DG, ASI issues a notice ordering the illegal occupant to vacate the occupied site and remove the encroachment.  If no action
 is taken by the encroacher, the DG, ASI issues an order under Section 19 (2) of the Ancient  Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958 and Rule 38 (2) of the Ancient
 Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Rules, 1959 to the Collector and the concerned district authorities for demolition and removal of the encroachment.  The Archaeological
 Survey of India also initiates legal action in the courts against the encroachers.  Though the Superintending Archaeologists have been vested with the power of Estate Officer and authorized
 to issue eviction notices under the Public Premises Eviction of Unauthorized Occupants (Act), 1971, the successful removal of encroachment depends upon  entirely on the cooperation of
 the police and district authorities, which is seldom forthcoming.   In the Delhi Circle specifically, there are encroachments on 14 centrally protected monuments and action is under way for
 their removal.  In the case of several encroachments, the matter is sub-judice in the courts of law.  In so far as the Siri Fort Wall is concerned, the protected  stretch of the fortification wall is
 free from encroachment, but a portion of the Siri Fort Wall, which is not under the protection of the Archaeological Survey of India and falling within Shahpur Jat Village, is encroached
 upon by the villagers.   There are two cases in the Court in respect of Siri Fort Wall.
29.       The Director-General, ASI during the course of oral evidence also submitted that  :
"Encroachment in and around ASI monuments is one of the problems ASI is facing.  3,658 monuments are protected.  If you put a reasonable number of people to protect it, it
 would require at least 7-8 thousand people.  If you take monuments like the Taj or Red Fort, each would take at least 200 people.  In fact, it is consuming one-third of the
 staff to protect just these two.  There is no physical protection at all and the encroachment is going on for several years.  We have powers to issue notice for the people to
 vacate.  But we don't have the power to compel them to vacate. This State Government police support hardly ever comes." 
 
30.       The Ministry of Culture informed the Committee that at present, there are 3463 Monument Attendants in Archaeological Survey of India.  CISF personal have been employed in Red
 Fort in Delhi and the Taj Mahal in Agra.  For 459 CISF personnel employed in these two sensitive monuments, the financial implication per year is Rs.9.25 crores.  Besides, 100 State
 Police personnel are being paid for deployment at some monuments and museums.  The total payment involved to the State Police personnel is Rs.1.5 crores annually.  However a large
 number of protected monuments all over the country are not having any security.  There is no precise estimate of the funds required for providing security guards to all these monuments. 
 However on purely tentative estimates, it is estimated that an amount of Rs.100 crores may be required annually for proper physical security to all the protected monuments by way of
 deploying private security guards.
31.       The Committee expresses its anxiety over the incidents of encroachment upon the land of Centrally Protected Monuments.  The Committee is more concerned about the inability of
 Archeological Survey of India to get back the land from encroachers.  Therefore, the Committee strongly recommends that a complete assessment should be made regarding encroachment
 of monuments/sites under the protection of Archaeological Survey of India all over the country.  Prompt action ought be taken against the encroachers with the help of State
 Governments/Local Administrations and the matter should be pursued at the highest level.  The Committee also recommends that adequate budgetary provisions should be made for security

 the schemes is that the quality of life of young people be made sensitive to what is aesthetically and morally good in our society. This can be done by exposing them to the finest forms of
 creative expression from an early age. Cultural complexes for children will provide these avenues for our young people. Multipurpose cultural complexes of general nature foster and
 coordinate activities in the state in the different cultural fields such as music, drama, dance, literature, fine arts etc. and promote through them the cultural unity of the country.

ZONAL CULTURAL CENTRES
75.       The Zonal Cultural Centres (ZCC) were created to promote cultural awareness and to identify, nurture and promote vanishing folk art traditions in the rural and semi urban areas. 
 The seven Zonal Cultural Centres, encompassing all the states and union territories of the country, were set up to extend local creative support to folk and traditional artisans of India.  Each
 Centre functions as an autonomous body, with the Governor of the State, where it is located serving as the ex officio  Chairman.  In Budget Estimate 2005-06 an amount of Rs.30 crore has
 been allocated to the Zonal Cultural Centres as against of Rs.19 crore allocated in RE 2004-05. The main source of income for meeting administrative expenditure of the ZCCs is the
 interest accrued on the  fixed deposits of the corpus fund.  The falling interest rate has resulted in the reduction of income from the corpus fund while expenditure on establishment costs
 have increased due to inflation, increase in artists remuneration, increase in salary etc.   To tide over the financial crises an allocation of Rs.35 crores was provided in 10
th Five Year Plan i.e.
 Rs.5 crores per ZCC for corpus fund.
76.       The corpus of the ZCCs were enhanced by Rs.5 crores each to boost their financial strength of which Rs.2 crores has already been released to each of ZCCs.   In the forthcoming
 financial year an additional corpus of Rs.3 crores will be sanctioned. In  view of the special status of NE States and the problem faced by NEZCC the total additional corpus of Rs.5 crores
 has already been released to them.  Further, an amount of Rs.15 lakhs for Shilpgram for each of the ZCCs will be sanctioned in the forthcoming financial year for their Shilpgram activities. 
77.       The Committee notes that Zonal Cultural Centres are playing important roles to create cultural awareness among the public specially in rural and semi urban areas.  The efforts of the
 Ministry to strengthen the Zonal Cultural Centres by enhancing the allocation is praise worthy.   The Committee directs the Ministry to ensure that the additional amount of Rs.5.00 crore
 released to North East Zonal Cultural Centres should be fully utilized by them.

th November,
 1996 on the basis of the recommendations of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource Development as contained in its 10 th Report.  This was done with the aim of
 mobilizing extra resources.  It was formally launched on 29 th March 1997.  The National Culture Fund aims at inviting the participation of the corporate sector, NGOs, State Governments,

 AT A GLANCE
 
The Committee is happy to note that the Ministry of Culture had proposed an outlay of Rs.551.12 crore and also got an approved outlay of the same amount with a capital component
 of Rs.61.80 crore.   The Committee hopes that the Ministry of Culture will be able to utilize the funds for implementation of new Schemes/Projects optimally. 
            The Committee, however, is not convinced about the reasons cited by the Ministry that budget was passed late and accordingly, there was shorter time available to spend the money
 allocated to them and observes that if the annual plan starts after the beginning of the financial year itself, then it considerably reduces the capacity of the Ministry to plan out expenditure.  
 Therefore, the planning for financial progress has to start even before as the broad heads are already known to the Ministry under the contours of the five-year plan.  The Committee also
 fails to understand as to how this intra-year financial development should deter the Ministry in planning it in such a manner that none of the financial allocations made can be successfully
 used by the end of the year.  Therefore, the Committee strongly recommends that the Finance Ministry recalling the money which has been already allocated is a serious problem and the
 Ministry should take adequate care and evolve a sound method of financial planning so that such kind of circumstance may never occur in future.
            The Committee notes that the Ministry of Culture this time has given more emphasis to various reputed institutes of art and culture like, Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies,
 Gandhi Smriti and Darshan Samiti, Buddhist and Tibetan Institutes, Multi Purpose Cultural Complexes, Ram Krishna Mission Institute of Culture, Kolkata, etc.  The Committee hopes that
 the construction of proposed new Multi Purpose Cultural Complexes in Manipur, Nagaland, Assam, Rajasthan, Chattisgarh  and Andhra Pradesh would be completed in time.  The
 Committee further directs that the additional amount of Rs.46 crore which has been for the first time provided for Centenaries and Anniversaries Celebration will be spent fairly and in an
 unbiased manner. The Committee also recommends that ongoing projects on publication of volumes of works of Lok Nayak Jaiprakash Narayan be completed in time and funds for that
 purpose will be provided as assured by the Ministry.    Moreover, Birth Anniversary Celebrations of Lok Nayak Jaiprakash Narayan and Choudhary Charan Singh should be continued
 every year.  The Committee strongly recommends that the entire provisions made by the Ministry of Culture be utilised during the year 2005-06.

 Financial year 2004-05, an outlay of Rs.1066.55 crore was allocated for the port sector but the ports could utilize only Rs.440.51 crore. The Committee is dismayed by this repeated failure
 of Department of Shipping and is surprised as to why the Ministry asks for so much of allocation if it is not in position to spend the approved outlay. The Committee desires that the
 Department of Shipping should take all corrective measures based upon actual requirements for maximum utilization of budgeted amount during 2005-06.  In this regard, the Committee
 reiterates its earlier recommendation contained in 81
st report of Demands for Grants (2004-05) of Ministry of Shipping which reads as under:-
"The Committee fails to understand as to how the physical targets will be achieved with this low utilization pattern.  In fact, the Committee feels that this raises doubts about
 the mismatch in the projections for physical and financial targets.  The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Shipping has full responsibility to ensure proper
