2.         At the outset the Committee enquired about the power and position of the North-Eastern Council and was there any significant change
after the enforcement of the North-Eastern Council (Amendment) Act, 2002.  The Committee was apprised by the representative of the NEC
that there is no significant change in their powers.  As per the Act, the council plays the role of an Advisory Body and may discuss any matter
in which some or all of the States represented in that council, or the Union and one or more of the States represented in that council, have a

common interest and advise the Central Government and the Government of each State concerned as to the action to be taken on any such
matter, and in particular, matters relating to economic and social planning, inter state transport and communications, matter relating to power or
flood control projects of common interest.  In order to give more powers to NEC, a high-powered Committee was constituted under the
Chairmanship of Shri P. P. Srivastava, which submitted its report on 
30
th
 July 2004
.  The representatives of the Ministry of North Eastern
Region informed that major recommendations of that Committee are yet to be implemented.  The Committee desired that this should be done at
the earliest. 
3.         The Committee was apprised by the NEC representatives in detail about the infrastructural problems in the region.  As regards the
roads, the Committee was apprised that due to inadequate allocation of fund, construction of Inter-state roads took long period of time. 
Secondly, the States are supposed to take over the roads on completion but they are not maintaining the roads due to lack of resources.  They
expressed that there is a need for reconciling and conflicting priority of inter-state roads constructed under NEC.  In addition to inadequate
funds, natural calamities caused by heavy rainfall and landslides also further deteriorate the linkage.  The NEC representatives stated that with
regards to civil aviation sector, air connectivity should be upgraded and improved.  In addition to the upgradation of airports, NEC has
supported procurement of four 50-seater Aircrafts through Alliance Air to improve air connectivity in the region at the cost of Rs.175.00 crore. 
However, the region continues to face connectivity problem due to withdrawal of bigger aircraft and increase in average waiting period.  The
Committee took note of all these issues and directed the concerned Ministry representative to take remedial measures and get back to the
Committee in this regard.

the Ministry of Civil Aviation and directed to furnish written replies in this regard.

9.         The Committee notes that Ministry of Civil Aviation has failed to fully utilize the outlay approved during 2004-
05.  The Ministry anticipates to utilize an amount of Rs.1473.03 crore out of the approved allocation of Rs.1620.98
 crore during the year 2004-05, which exemplifies the poor financial management in the Ministry of Civil Aviation.  The
 Committee feels that there is a lack of proper planning in the various organisations of Ministry of Civil Aviation, as a
 result of which the Ministry was unable to utilize optimally the approved outlays at its disposal.  The Committee,
 therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Civil Aviation should impress upon the concerned agencies to make a
 realistic assessment of their financial requirements so that the allocations made do not remain unutilized. 
ANALYSIS OF THE AVIATION POLICY
10.       The Committee notes that the civil aviation sector has grown in the country during the recent years.  As per the
 aviation policy being pursued by the Government, the Ministry of Civil Aviation has taken a number of steps which
 have affected the airlines and the airports in the country.  The Government has taken decision to allow Air India and
 Indian Airlines to proceed with the acquisition process of aircraft. The Government has allowed private domestic
 carriers to fly on international routes also.  With respect to the airport sector, the Government has taken steps for
 modernization and restructuring of the Delhi and Mumbai airports.  The Government has also taken steps towards the
 development of Greenfield airports at Bangalore and Hyderabad. 
 
11.       The aviation policy being pursued by the Government will have a bearing on the various aspects of the civil
 aviation sector in the country in general and the public sector airline companies in particular.   The Committee analysed
 the effect of the aviation policy of the various aspects of the civil aviation sector such as opening of international routes
 to private airlines, requirement of trained manpower, infrastructure and maintenance facilities at airports, modernization
 and restructuring of the Delhi and Mumbai airports, development of Greenfield airports at Bangalore and Hyderabad,
 high cost of air turbine fuel (ATF), review of Route Dispersal Guidelines, impact of Fringe Benefit Tax, requirement of
 an eastern hub at Kolkata etc. The details of the analysis of the Committee have been discussed in the succeeding
 paragraphs of the report.

16.       The Committee noted that the Net Profit of Indian Airlines was estimated to go down from Rs.44.17 crore in
 2003-04 to Rs.8.75 crore in 2004-05 and the projection for 2005-06 was merely Rs.11.35 crore.  The Committee

 improve their position during 2005-06.

 Internal and Extra Budgetary Resources (IEBR) for the year 2004-05 had been compiled by Indian Airlines (IAL) in the
 month of October 2004, on the basis of costs prevalent at that time, wherein a Net Profit of Rs 8.75 crore had been
 projected.  However, the Net Profit of Rs.8.75 crore was lower than Rs.44.17 crore in 2003-04 due to increase in the

 early decision in the matter so that the employees of Indian Airlines are not deprived of their legitimate right to the
 revision of scales of pay which has been pending for long.

OPENING OF INTERNATIONAL ROUTES FOR PRIVATE AIRLINES
 
30.       During the course of the oral evidence of the Secretary and other officers of the Ministry of Civil Aviation held
 on the 30 th March 2005, the Committee drew the attention of the Secretary to the reports appearing in the press
 regarding the sequence of events in allowing private domestic airlines to fly on international routes.  The Committee
 pointed out that the decision of the Government to allow a particular airline to fly to international routes immediately
 preceeded the Initial Public Offer (IPO) of that airline. The Committee observed that the simultaneous timing of the
 decision of the Government and the respone of the public to the IPO of that company put a question mark on the
 Government policy of allowing private domestic carriers to fly on international routes.  The Committee briefly brought
 out the sequence of events in this episode.  First, the Cabinet decided on 29th December 2004 to allow some domestic
 private airlines to fly on international routes.  Within a few days, news appeared that a particular airline company
 would bring IPO in the market.  Thereafter, within one month of actual submission of the proposal to the SEBI by the
 company, the whole matter was considered by the Government. Thereafter, the Government announced the
 international routes to be awarded to the airline.  The Committee also pointed out that there were also some disturbing
 news reports regarding the manner in which the airline succeeded in securing the international routes it was permitted
 to fly.  The Committee sought the comments of Ministry of Civil Aviation on the points highlighted by the Committee.

REVIEW OF ROUTE DISPERSAL GUIDELINES
40.       The Committee had, in its 78
th Report on Demands for Grants 2004-05 of the Ministry of Civil Aviation
 observed that like Indian Airlines, private airlines should also fulfil their social commitments and not prefer to operate
 mostly on lucrative routes and complete the formality of fulfilling their social obligation by flying to the prescribed
 minimum flights to the North-East region under the Route Dispersal Guidelines.  The Committee had noted that Route
 Dispersal Guidelines had been manipulated by the private airlines to the disadvantage of the backward regions.   The
 Committee had recommended that the Ministry of Civil Aviation should evolve some mechanism to ensure that private
 airlines in the country fulfil their social obligation by operating more number of flights in the North-East region.  The
 Committee had also expressed the view that the Route Dispersal Guidelines should be reviewed with a view to making
 them full proof so that no private airline is able to violate them and any such violation should entail heavy disincentive
 to that airline.
 
41.       In their Action Taken Replies furnished to the Committee, the Ministry of Civil Aviation informed the
 Committee that the Ministry had constituted a Committee under the Chairmanship of DGCA vide  order dated 23-09-
2003 to review the Route Dispersal Guidelines.  The Committee had been mandated to submit its report within two
 months of issue of the order.  The review committee and its members had been provided with the contents of the
 observations of the Committee in this regard so as to incorporate these views while reviewing the present Route
 Dispersal Guidelines.  The committee had been requested to expedite its report.  During the course of the examination
 of Demands for Grants 2005-06 of the Ministry of Civil Aviation, it was informed that the Committee under DGCA to
 review the Route Dispersal Guidelines had submitted its report on 18.3.2005 which was being examined. 
 
42.       The Committee is of the view that the present aviation policy being followed by the Government has not been
 effective in making the private airlines share the social obligations of the country.  The Committee feels that the private
 airlines have been focusing on lucrative trunk routes only.  These airlines have been operating only on the basis of
 commercial terms and tend to follow the bare minimum of what is mandatory for them under the Route Dispersal
 Guidelines. The Committee recommends that the Route Dispersal Guidelines should be revisited to ensure that the
 private domestic airlines also share the social obligation of connecting remote parts of the country in the true sense and
 not by merely completing the formalities in this regard.

REVAMPING OF TRANSPORT SECTOR IN ANDAMAN AND NICOBAR ISLANDS IN POST TSUNAMI
 SCENARIO
 
129.     On an invitation of Lt. Governor, Andaman & Nicobar Islands, the Chairman, Committee on Transport, Tourism
 and Culture had visited the Islands to have discussion on revamping of Tourism and Transport Sectors in Andaman &
 Nicobar Islands in Post Tsunami Scenario. In the light of the above discussions, the Committee enquired from the
 Ministry of Civil Aviation as to why the Ministry of Civil Aviation was not introducing direct flights to Port Blair from
 other stations in the country apart from Kolkata and Chennai.  In response, the Committee was informed that Indian
 Airlines had been providing air services to Port Blair from Chennai and Kolkata for the past many decades.  Over the
 period of time, Chennai has come to be accepted as a gateway point for travel to Port Blair from South, West as well as
 North India, while Kolkata serves as gateway to Port Blair from East and North India.  Both Chennai and Kolkata are
 as such serving as hub points for operations to Port Blair.  Indian Airlines provides a daily over night connection to Port
 Blair over Chennai/ Kolkata and same day connection in the return direction.  While it would be ideal to have a same
 day onward connection to Port Blair, due to the limitations of Port Blair airfield, the same is not possible and the
 operations to/from Port Blair have to be restricted to morning hours.  In Indian Airlines’ estimate, the existing traffic
 potential to Port Blair from metros such as Delhi and Mumbai and other points is not sufficient to sustain direct services
 with the jet type of aircraft in Indian Airlines fleet.  Also Indian Airlines fleet is fully committed for operating on the
 existing schedule and spare capacity is not available to consider introduction of flights on new domestic routes. 
 Further, Government has laid down Route Dispersal Guidelines with a view to achieve better regulation of air transport
 services taking into account the need for air transport services of different regions of the country.  It is, however, up to
 the airlines to provide air services to specific places depending upon the traffic demand and commercial viability As
 such, the airlines are free to operate anywhere in the country subject to compliance of Route Dispersal Guidelines
 issued by the Government. However, all scheduled domestic airlines have been requested to consider this proposal.
 
130.     The Committee also desired to know as to when Ministry of Civil Aviation planned to allow the airlines
 operating to and from South and South East Asian countries to stop over at Port Blair airport, thereby opening the
 Islands to more tourists.  In response, the Committee was informed that designated airlines of all ASEAN countries,
 i.e., Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, Myanmar, Vietnam, Brunei, Philippines, Cambodia & Lao PDR as well
 as Sri Lanka have been permitted unlimited access to Port Blair.  Actual operations are, however, matters of
 commercial judgment of the airlines concerned.

 versa sector.  The APEX fares have been offered under three date slabs i.e.   D-7, D-21 and D-28.  The APEX fares

135.     During the visit, the Committee was apprised by the officials of the Ministry of Civil Aviation that as per the
 Rule 134 of Aircraft Rules, 1937, Route Dispersal Guidelines (RDG) have been issued by the Ministry and accordingly

 with these regions (Cat-II routes).  The Committee enquired from the Ministry about the reason as to why private

 care of and Route Dispersal Guidelines will be revised very soon.  The Committee is of the view that because of the
 difficult terrain and inaccessibility of the region by road, there exists a strong requirement for more flight-connectivity
 to all north-eastern States, though some of these airports are non profit making destinations. Accordingly, the
 Committee recommends that the private operators should also share the social obligation and provide more flights to all
 destinations instead of just fulfilling the existing minimum requirements of Route Dispersal Guidelines.

 crore during the year 2004-05, which exemplifies the poor financial management in the Ministry of Civil Aviation.  The
 Committee feels that there is a lack of proper planning in the various organisations of Ministry of Civil Aviation, as a
 result of which the Ministry was unable to utilize optimally the approved outlays at its disposal.  The Committee,
 therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Civil Aviation should impress upon the concerned agencies to make a
 realistic assessment of their financial requirements so that the allocations made do not remain unutilized.

ANALYSIS OF THE AVIATION POLICY
 
            The Committee would like to record its appreciation regarding the role played by Indian Airlines and Alliance
 Air in evacuation of people from Andaman & Nicobar Islands after the tsunami disaster and heavy snowfall in parts of
 Jammu & Kashmir in the winter season this year.  The Committee notes that Indian Airlines is expected to earn a profit
 of Rs.8.75 crore by the end of the financial year 2004-05.  The Committee understands the reasons for the low amount
 of profit likely to be earned by Indian Airlines.  The Committee observes that Indian Airlines does not have sufficient
 number of aircraft to optimally utilize the domestic seat capacity available in the country and the average age of the
 aircraft available with Indian Airlines is on the higher side.  Also Indian Airlines has to take the lion's share in
 undertaking social responsibilities of the nation.  As part of its social obligation, Indian Airlines also has to fly to those
 unremunerative destinations, which other airlines choose not to fly due to commercial considerations.  The Committee,
 therefore, appreciates that, inspite of the odds being placed heavily against the company, Indian Airlines would be
 ending the financial year 2004-05 with marginal profits.
 
            The Committee notes that the revision of scales of pay of employees of Indian Airlines had become due on
 1.1.1997.  However, even after a lapse of a period of more than eight years, the Government is yet to take a decision in
 the matter.  The Committee feels that the revision of scales of pay would contribute towards preventing the exodus of
 trained manpower from Indian Airlines. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should take an
 early decision in the matter so that the employees of Indian Airlines are not deprived of their legitimate right to the
 revision of scales of pay which has been pending for long.
 
            The Committee observes that the issues relating to acquisition of aircraft for Indian Airlines has been lingering

OPENING OF INTERNATIONAL ROUTES FOR PRIVATE AIRLINES
 
            The Committee is not convinced with the reply given by the Ministry of Civil Aviation regarding its decision to
 open up international skies to a particular airline and granting it passage rights to some international routes on the
 opening day of its public offer.  The Committee is of the view that the timing of the decision pushed up the company's
 IPO prospects and the policy adopted by the Government and the clearances granted by the Ministry to the company
 were too close to the public offer of the company to be termed as coincidence.  The Committee feels that grant of
 speedy clearances to the company helped the airline get a good opening for its equity offering.  The Committee is,
 therefore, of the view that the conduct of Ministry of Civil Aviation in granting speedy clearances to the airline and the
 policy changes should be further enquired into by an independent agency.
 
            The Committee is not convinced with the reply furnished by Ministry of Civil Aviation with regard to the
 criteria adopted in selection of scheduled domestic airlines to be allowed to fly on international routes.  The Committee
 feels that there is an element of arbitrariness in imposing restrictions on airlines in terms of experience of flying etc.
 and not allowing all the domestic scheduled airlines to fly on international routes. By imposing such restrictions, the
 Ministry of Ministry of Civil Aviation did not give a fair chance to the other scheduled domestic private airline
 operating in the country. The Committee is also of the view that Ministry of Civil Aviation did not carry out any due
 diligence of the performance record of the existing private sector airlines in terms of fulfilling the social obligations by
 flying to remote and inaccessible areas of the country and utilizing the costly technologies installed at the airports such
 as ILS CAT-III system.
 
            The Committee notes that there is a contradiction between the objectives stated by the Ministry of Civil Aviation
 in allowing private airlines to fly to international destinations and the routes actually allotted by the Ministry of Civil
 Aviation to the private airlines. The Committee observes that the basic objective of the Government in allowing private
 airlines to fly to international destinations was providing connectivity to such destinations which the Ministry had not
 been able to provide in the past because of lack of capacity of Air India and Indian Airlines.  However, the Ministry of
 Civil Aviation has granted permission to these private airlines to fly to those destinations which were already being
 serviced by Air India and Indian Airlines.  Hence the stated position of the Government in this respect is in total
 contradiction with the actual decisions of the Government and the basic objective of the Government to provide
 connectivity to new international destinations has been defeated.
(Paras 32, 35 and 39)
REVIEW OF ROUTE DISPERSAL GUIDELINES
            The Committee is of the view that the present aviation policy being followed by the Government has not been
 effective in making the private airlines share the social obligations of the country.  The Committee feels that the private
 airlines have been focusing on lucrative trunk routes only.  These airlines have been operating only on the basis of
 commercial terms and tend to follow the bare minimum of what is mandatory for them under the Route Dispersal
 Guidelines. The Committee recommends that the Route Dispersal Guidelines should be revisited to ensure that the
 private domestic airlines also share the social obligation of connecting remote parts of the country in the true sense and
 not by merely completing the formalities in this regard.
 (Para 42)
REQUIREMENT OF TRAINED MANPOWER
            The Committee is of the view that as per the policy being pursued by the Government in granting licenses to
 new private airlines, a lot of investment is coming in the airline industry.  Vast expansion of fleet is also taking place in
 the existing national and private carriers.  The Committee feels that there is a mismatch between the pace at which the
 airline fleet is expanding and the human resource being groomed for the same thereby, resulting in tremendous shortage
 of trained manpower.  The Committee recommends that Ministry of Civil Aviation should undertake an objective
 assessment of the requirement of trained manpower for civil aviation sector as a whole in the country on priority basis.

 that the investment made by the Government on training of such manpower is not utilized by private airlines at the cost

UNDERUTILISATION OF ILS CAT-III SYSTEM INSTALLED AT INDIRA GANDHI INTERNATIONAL

            The Committee is constrained to note that while the current policy of the Government aims at allowing more and
 more airlines to operate in the country, it has not made it obligatory for them to utilize the modern facilities installed at

 three private airlines i.e. Jet Airways, Sahara Airlines and Air Deccan have not trained any of their pilots for CAT-III
 operations and there is no legal requirement in the Aircraft Rules and Civil Aviation requirements to make it mandatory
 for private airlines to train their pilots on ILS CAT-III System.  The Committee is also not satisfied with the progress
 achieved with respect to the training of the pilots by the National Carriers viz. Indian Airlines and Air India, for
 utilizing the CAT-III System.  The Committee recommends that in order to improve the operational efficiency during
 the extreme foggy conditions, the Ministry should amend 'Aircraft Rules' to incorporate a provision for making training
 of pilots compulsory by the private airlines on CAT-III System so that the investment made by the Government on the
 installation of the system through the tax payers' money is not underutilized.   The Committee hopes that the national
 carriers and the private airlines will optimally utilize the ILS CAT-III System installed in the IGI Airport, New Delhi
 during the period of poor visibility, which will certainly reduce the hardships faced by the passengers.

ALLOTMENT OF PARKING BAYS
            The Committee is constrained to note that before giving licenses to new airlines to commence operations, the
 Government did not deliberate on the infrastructure and maintenance facilities required at the airports after these

            The Committee is of the view that, as brought out by the Ministry of Civil Aviation, the proposals of Fringe

            The Committee observes that the withdrawal of Income Tax exemption on payment of lease rentals of
 aircraft/aircraft engines will, in particular, adversely affect Air India and Indian Airlines as they have a significant
 portion of their fleet as leased aircraft, which are due for renewal and are also planning to induct additional aircraft
 through lease.  Alliance Air, a subsidiary of Indian Airlines is also planning to commence replacement of ageing fleet
 initially through lease route.  Similarly, Air India plans to establish a low cost airline named Air India Express by
 leasing aircraft.  The withdrawal of this facility will also pose an entry barrier to new airlines planning to introduce low
 cost operations as most of these airlines plan to induct aircraft initially through lease route.  All these new initiatives
 will be adversely affected with the withdrawal of income tax exemption, which was available to payment of lease

 huge difference in the figures quoted by the Ministry.  The Committee also regrets to note that the Ministry has not

CREATION OF A EASTERN HUB AT KOLKATA
            The Committee is of the opinion that with the growth of the aviation sector in the country, the pressure and strain
 on Mumbai and Delhi airports is also increasing.  The Committee is apprehensive that with the arrival of private players
 in the airline sector, there will be a further intensification of this pressure.  As accepted by the Secretary of the Ministry,
 the Delhi and Mumbai-centric activity was also becoming unmanageable.  Therefore there exists a need to develop
 alternate destinations, particularing in the eastern part of country.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that Ministry
 of Civil Aviation should take steps for the creation of an eastern hub at Kolkata.  The Committee also notes that while a
 foreign carrier was fully exploiting the availability of air traffic in Kolkata, our own carriers did not even have a
 presence there. The Committee, therefore, also recommends that Ministry of Civil Aviation should introduce
 international flights from Kolkata.  In the context of look East policy of the Government, the Committee feels that
 locational advantage of Kolkata vis-à-vis South East and Far East Asia can be leveraged. Apart from this, the
 Committee feels that this will reduce the pressure on Delhi & Mumbai airports to a great extent.  On similar grounds,
 the Committee also feels that a Southern hub should be established at Chennai.

 services in the Domestic Sector for short-haul distances.  The Committee feels that there is a need for reinventing Air

 growth.   The Committee recommends that the Ministry should explore the possibility for providing regular air
 transport services by PHHL to connect specific places, especially hilly areas which are inaccessible by a fixed wing

 review the Guidelines. They also stated that Naresh Chandra Committee had also recommended for this.  They assured

 whereas, the total number of visitors is approximately 4500-6000 per month.  The total number of aircraft movements
 are 46 per week by scheduled operators, i.e. Indian Airlines, Alliance Air and Jet Airways.  The B.S.F. and Indian Air
 Force are operating non-scheduled flights frequently including AVRO, IL76, AN32 and helicopter movements.  The
 Committee was further apprised that the Imphal Airport is equipped with all modern navigational facilities like
 Instrument Landing System (CAT-I) on Runway on VOR/DME, NDB, PAPI and Approach Lighting System.  The
 Runway length is 9010 ft. which is capable of handling Airbus-320 and Boeing 737-800 series aircrafts without any
 load restrictions.  The Runway 04 is the Precision Approach Runway equipped with ILS whereas Runway 22 is the
 usual runway.  Recently, the New Taxiway and Apron was constructed which can accommodate 4 aircraft (1 ATR, IB-
737, Indian Airlines -320, Indian Airlines -300).  Also the Isolation Bay has been constructed and commissioned at
 Imphal Airport for any eventuality. 
 
5.         The Chairman of the Committee emphasised that while constructing the terminal building local art and
 architecture should be kept in mind and building should be designed accordingly.  Civil Aviation and Tourism go hand

 Navigation Surveillance, Fire and Rescue Service (Cat-5 Cat-6) are provided as per International (ICAO)
 specifications.  The total officers and staff strength available at Imphal under AAI is 120 with various disciplines like
 Air Traffic Control, Communication Navigation Surveillance, HRD, Fire and Rescue Services.  The conservancy is
 given a contract through AMC which is well-maintained through modern equipments.

R E P O R T
 
The Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Bill, 2004 seeks to address the issue of security pertaining to the
 Merchant Shipping in India and to amend the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and Indian Ports Act, 1908 so as to
 incorporate therein provisions relating to security measures to be adopted by ships and port, port facilities, ship
 identification number, port facility assessment, international ship security certificate, ship security alert system, control
 measures and compliance.
 
2.                     The statement of objects and reasons of the Bill states that India has ratified the International Convention
 on Safety of Life at Sea 1974 (SOLAS 1974) on 16
th June 1976, which came into force on 25 th May 1980.  This
 Convention in its successive forms is generally regarded as the most important of all international treaties concerning
 the safety of merchant ships.  The main objective of the SOLAS 1974 is to specify minimum standards for the
 construction, equipment and operation of ships, compatible with their safety.  There are 11 codes or similar instruments
 that are made mandatory under SOLAS 1974.  Of these, the last Code is the 'International Code for the Security of
 Ships and Port Facility' (ISPS Code).  This Code was adopted as an amendment to SOLAS 1974 by the conference of
 contracting States on 12
th December 2002, by passing 11 resolutions.  Out of those 11 Resolutions, Resolution No. 6
 inter-alia prescribes 1st July 2004 as the application dates for the code.  If the ISPS Code is not implemented it will be
 difficult for the Indian Ships to secure entry in the Ports of other contracting States an also for the foreign ships to visit
 Indian Ports.
 
3.
                                         The statement of objects and reasons of the Bill further states that with a view to implement the
 provisions of the ISPS Code, it is proposed to amend the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.  India being a major seafarer-
supplying nation, it is essential to ensure that our seafarers' employment prospects and movements to other countries are
 not hampered for want of Seafarers' identity document.  Accordingly, it is proposed to incorporate necessary provisions
 in the Bill.
4.
                                         The statement of objects and reasons of the Bill also states that since the implementation of ISPS Code
 also involves ports, it is proposed to consequentially amend the Indian Ports Act, 1908 so as to facilitate a port facility
 in complying with the requirements of the maritime security proposed to be included under the new Part IX B of the

89th Report of Committee on T & T
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/89threport.htm[22-10-2018 12:09:16]
 Merchant Shipping act, 1958.
 
5.                                         In their background note furnished to the Committee giving the reasons for the introduction of the Bill,
 the Department of Shipping have brought out in the succeeding paragraphs:-
 
NEED FOR ISPS CODE
5.1                   Part IX of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 relates to 'Safety' of ships.  The provisions of this part
 achieves implementation of International Convention on Safety of Life at sea, 1974 (SOLAS 1974), which came into
 force internationally on 25
th May 1980. India having ratified this on 16 th June 1976 the convention came into force in
 India on 25 th May 1980.  The main objective of the SOLAS Convention is to specify minimum standards for the
 construction, equipment and operation of ships, compatible with their safety.  The Convention has been updated and
 amended on numerous occasions hence is referred to as SOLAS 1974, as amended.  There are 11 Codes or similar
 instruments that are made mandatory under SOLAS 1974.  Of these the last Code is 'International Code for the Security
 of Ships and of port Facility' (ISPS Code).  Following the tragic events of 11 th September 2001, the 22nd session of the
 Assembly of the IMO in November 2001 had unanimously agreed to the development of new measures relating to the
 security of ships and of port facilities for adoption by a Conference of Contracting Governments to the SOLAS 1974. 
 This Code was adopted as an amendment to SOLAS by the conference of Contracting Governments (SOLAS 1974) on
 12th December 2002.  To address the issue of 'Security' in the legislation pertaining to merchant shipping in India, it has
 been proposed to introduce/insert a new part IXB in the Merchant Shipping Act along with minor changes in the long
 title of the Act, new definition of security in Section 3 in part I, amendment of section 31 in Part V.  To complement the
 provisions of new part IXB it was also felt necessary to make corresponding amendments in Indian Ports Act, 1908 by
 providing new Section 68 D.
 
OBJECTIVES OF ISPS CODE
5.2                   The objectives of the ISPS Code are to establish an international framework-involving co-operation
 between contracting States, Government agencies, local administrations and the shipping and port industries to detect
 or assess security threats and take preventive measures against security incidents affecting ships or port facilities used
 in international trade; to establish the respective roles and responsibilities of all concerned at the national and
 international level for ensuring maritime security; to ensure the early and efficient colletion and  exchange of security
 related information; to provide a methodology for security assessments so as to have in place plans and procedures to
 react to changing security levels and; to ensure adequate and proportionate maritime security measures.  If the ISPS
 Code is not implemented, it will be difficult for the Indian ships to secure entry in the ports of other contracting states
 and also for the foreign ships to visit Indian ports. Therefore, it was felt necessary to provide legislative support to
 Indian ships in respect of security and to provide corresponding measures at Indian ports for foreign flag ships.

5.3                   Similarly, 'Seafarers Identity Document Convention (Revised), 2003', (Convention 185) was adopted by
 International Labour Conference, Geneva, on 19th June 2003.  According to this, access to ships/ports will be restricted
 to only those seafarers who are in possession of Seafarers Identity Document.  Therefore, to bring the Indian seafarers
 at par with international standards, it was felt necessary to introduce corresponding changes in the Merchant Shipping
 Act by insertion of new section 99A in Part VII.  Since India is a major seafarer-supplying nation to international
 shipping, it is imperative that the Indian seafarers are issued the identification documents giving his biometrics and
 personal information, which can be scrutinized, from any port of world for its genuineness.  These provisions would
 ensure that employment opportunity of Indian Seafarers is not compromised.  Similar checks have been employed for
 foreign seafarers at Indian ports at the facilities to meet the requirements of this convention and ensure security of our
 ports and country at large. 
 
SCOPE OF ISPS CODE
6.                                         The scope of ISPS Code is limited to ship and port facilities and the measures included in the Code are
 essentially preventive measures so as to reduce the chances of easy entry for unlawful elements such as and they have
 to be implemented by the port security personnel and the trained ship-staff.  Further, in case of any security incident,
 there would be a better coordination with the agencies in-charge of security and the law and other in the area.  There
 would also be a better awareness towards ensuring safety of ships from acts of sabotage etc.  The measures will also
 ensure that the ships and ports would not be a soft target of the terrorists besides introducing some security measures
 which would assist the port and ship staff in preventing unauthorized entry in ports and on board ships, there are other
 measures to ensure that weapons and unauthorized people are not permitted to enter the port or ships through
 cargo/stores or otherwise.  This necessitates that the port facilities where the ship port interface takes place are
 sanitized.
 
FEATURES OF ISPS CODE
7.                                         The salient features of the ISPS code are as under:-
Ž         To establish an international framework involving co-operation between contracting Governments,
 Government agencies, local administrations and the shipping and port industries to detect and assess
 security threats and take preventive measures against security incidents affecting ships or port facilities
 used in international trade.
Ž          To establish the respective roles and responsibilities of the Contracting Governments, Government
 agencies, local administration and the shipping and port industries, at the national and international level,
 for ensuring maritime security.
Ž         To ensure the early and efficient collection and exchange of security-related information.
Ž         To provide a methodology for security assessments so as to have in place plans and procedures to react to
 changing security levels and

89th Report of Committee on T & T
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/89threport.htm[22-10-2018 12:09:16]
Ž         To ensure confidence that adequate and proportionate maritime security measures are in place.
 
FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS OF ISPS CODE
8.                     In order to achieve its objectives, this code embodies a number of functional requirements.  These
 include, but are not limited to:-
Ž                Gathering and assessing information with respect to security threats and exchanging such information
 with appropriate contracting Governments;
Ž                Requiring the maintenance of communication protocols for ships and port facilities;
Ž                Preventing unauthorized access to ships, port facilities and their restricted areas;
Ž                Preventing the introduction of unauthorized weapons, incendiary devices or explosives to ships or port
 facilities;
Ž                Providing means for raising the alarm in reaction to security threats or security incidents;
Ž                Requiring ship and port facility security plans based upon security assessments; and
Ž                Requiring training, drills and exercises to ensure familiarity with security plans and procedures.
APPLICATION OF ISPS CODE
9.                     The ISPS Code shall apply to the following type of ships on International
Voyages and Port Facilities serving such ships:-
Ž                Passengers ships irrespective of size,
Ž                Cargo ships of 500 Gross Tonnage and above not on International voyage.
Ž                All ships of 300 Gross Tonnage on International voyages
Ž                 Port facility serving ships on International voyages.
Ž                Mobile of shore Drilling Units.

16.                The Department of Shipping further informed the Committee that ISPS Code has come into existence through

 16th June 1976.  The aforesaid amendments were deemed to have been accepted on 1st January 2004 unless prior to that

 fleet of which constitute not less than 50% of the gross tonnage of the world's merchant fleet have notified their
 objections to the amendments.  Since this has not happened, amendments to SOLAS have come into effect.  Since ISPS
 Code is being implemented under this amendment to SOLAS, no fresh ratification is required.  The present amendment
 Bill is to give legislative backup to ISPS Code.  Therefore, there is no encroachment upon the law making powers of

FORMATION OF MARITIME SECURITY ADVISORY COMMITTEE 
18.                   As regards involvement of Merchant Shipping into the business of security, which is essentially the job
 of the Naval Force or the Armed Forces and formation of a Maritime Security Advisory Committee under the Ministry
 of Defence, the Department of Shipping vide their O.M. dated 17.02.2005 informed the Committee that the role of
 Naval forces or the Armed forces is in no way perceived to be different post-ISPS Code implementation.  In fact,
 International Maritime Organization is not the body to deliberate upon the role of Armed forces in relation to their
 sovereign powers in protecting their national security interests and therefore the Code had no intention to discuss such
 issues.  As already stated, the scope of the ISPS Code and the SOLAS chapter XI-2, based on which the Merchant
 Shipping (Amendment) Bill, 2004 has been prepared, is confined to only preventive measures to deter and detect.  It is
 clarified that the objective of the code is to establish an international frame work involving cooperation between
 contracting Governments, Government agencies, local administrations, shipping and the port industry to detect security
 threats and take preventive measures against security incidents affecting ships or port facilities only.  The role of
 Armed forces is to respond to any security incident, which may be reported by the ships or port facilities.  Hence the
 objective of ISPS Code in no way clashes with already established role of law enforcement agencies, naval forces or the
 armed forces.  Moreover, jurisdiction of coast guard and navy commences outside the port limit whereas the ISPS Code
 is concerned with port facility security, which is always inside the port limit.  Port Security in the country has been
 traditionally covered by the CISF, Port Police, State Police and in some cases by Private Security i.e. very similar to the
 practice followed by Airports. Port & Ship Security involves screening the cargo, access control, ship port interface and
 interaction with custom etc.  All such issues come under the control of Civilian Authorities.

 implementation of ISPS Code to ports of the country.  For this purpose, a new section 68D is intended to be inserted in
 Indian Ports Act, 1908.   The proposed amendment will not have any adverse impact on the employees of ports.  On the
 contrary, it will instill greater awareness amongst them about the maritime security concerns.  Further, the present Bill
 will also not interfere in the working of the employees of the ports and implementation of ISPS Code does not hamper
 the interest of employees in any manner.  On the contrary, the security aspects will further add quality to the work
 involvement of the employees. There are no provisions proposed or intended in the Amendments, which may go
 against the employees of the port or impinge upon any commercial or trade union activities.
 
45.                   The Committee notes that the present Bill broadly has been brought before the Parliament with a view to
 implement ISPS Code in the Ships and Ports facilities and hopes that as it has been assured by the Department of
 Shipping also that the proposed amendments neither have any adverse impact on the employees of ports nor impinge
 upon any commercial or trade union activities.  The Committee, however, have doubts that in the name of the security,
 trade union activities may be checked. The Committee therefore recommends that the employees/Unions of the major
 ports should not be made victims on account of proposed maritime security measures observed at the port & ships and
 the trade unions rights should also be protected and if necessary, a provision for protecting the interest of the employees

 and legitimate trade union activities should also be incorporated in the bill itself.
SHORE LEAVE
46.                   The Committee desires to know from the Department of Shipping as to how the human element related
 aspects will be taken care of under the ISPS regime and what are provisions for shore leave for seafarers who go on
 voyages of very long duration.  During the course of evidence tendered on 23.02.2005, the Secretary of Department of
 Shipping deposed before the Committee that; 
"Sir, on shore leave, I fully agree with you.  There is a resolution of the IMO also on this that human element
 must be taken into consideration.  In India, you would not find where we have denied shore leave to any other
 flagship.  We are quite humane in that regard.  In difficulty or in terms of illness to the seafarers, our ports'
 people immediately help them.  When our seafarers go to other countries, they are not given that shore leave. 
 After the September 11 event, they say, "No".  The ILO has also considered this issue and we are also putting
 these things before the Member countries.  In India, of course, the human element will be the foremost.  So far,
 the Ministry has not received any complaint. But if you have any suggestions on it, we will welcome that."
 
47.                   The Committee notes with anguish that 'human element' has not been given due consideration in the Bill
 and no provision has been made to see that the seafarers are granted leave under the ISPS security regime.  The
 Committee is of the opinion that shore leave is absolutely imperative from the humanitarian point of view.  The
 Committee recommends that shore leave be institutionalized within the framework of law and a clause be inserted in
 the proviso to section 344 (M).

48.                   The Committee recommends that the Bill be passed after incorporating official amendments and taking
 into account its recommendation in respect of Sections 3(44A), 344L, 344Q and 344J of the bill along with the
 recommendations contained in paras 14, 17, 23, 25, 29, 37, 45 and 47 above.

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS
AT A GLANCE
 
REASONS FOR ADOPTION OF ISPS CODE AND PROTECTION OF NATIONAL INTEREST
 
The Committee takes note of the fact that in order to ensure continuity of EXIM trade the Government has entered into
 this agreement.  The Committee agrees with the views of the Government that if the ISPS Code is not implemented the
 Indian ships & port facilities may act as a non-tariff barrier for sea borne commerce. It appears to the Committee that
 current assessment of security threat to shipping sector is basically the consequence of 9/11 attack on U.S.A.  Terrorism
 has a much longer history, however, International Maritime Organization ignored that fact and suddenly woke up to the
 threat of security and agreed unanimously to the evolution of new measures relating to ships and port facilities post
 9/11.  The Committee does not approve the contention of the Secretary that the ISPS Code provides both voluntary as
 well as mandatory provisions.  The Committee feels that security perception is a sovereign function and it is country
 specific. It is not fair, therefore, to confuse between our own security requirements and demands of international trade. 
 Protecting the nation, is a sovereign function of the Government. The Committee, therefore, recommends the
 Department of Shipping to look into the national priorities and interests while implementing the ISPS code.
 (Para 14)
 
ENCROACHING UPON THE LAW MAKING POWERS OF THE PARLIAMENT

The Committee recognizes that our constitution empowers the Government to enter into international agreements and no
 subsequent ratification by the Parliament is necessary.  However, if such agreements warrant any legislative change
 subsequently, then powers of the Parliament are final.  Therefore, the Government should be mindful of that flexibility.
(Para 17)
 
FORMATION OF MARITIME SECURITY ADVISORY COMMITTEE
 
The Committee notes that IMO is not the body to deliberate upon the role of Armed forces in relation to their sovereign
 powers in protecting their national security interest and the scope of ISPS Code is confined to only preventive measures
 to deter and detect and the role of armed forces is to respond to any security incident reported by ships or port facilities.
 The Committee feels that the problem of security is very old and the security requirements are becoming far too
 complex to be handled in the manner they were being handled in the past.  Therefore, an international organisation
 which is primarily engaged in commercial activity through sea route should not have been involved in the business of
 security and some defence related agencies i.e. Navy and Armed forces should have essentially dealt with this kind of a
 code.  The Committee therefore, recommends for creation of a Maritime Security Advisory Committee to report on and
 make recommendations on National Maritime Security matter under the Ministry of Defence so that all commerce
 handled by the Port and Ships would achieve appropriate security coverage.
 (Para 23)
 
COMPETENCE OF PORT AUTHORITY TO ADDRESS SECURITY ISSUES
 
The Committee notes that the port authorities are competent to address the security issue so far as terrorist activities are
 concerned. But, the existing practices on ships and port facilities security are not considered adequate at the
 international level. The Committee, however, recommends that all port facilities and Indian vessels should have
 comprehensive security plans that are evolved by port authorities and shipping companies in conjunction with the
 Indian Navy and the Coast Guard besides setting up local port security committees for better coordination of efforts of
 central, state and local law enforcement and security agencies.
(Para 25)
 
AUTHORITY FOR TAKING DECISION ON THE SECURITY PERCEPTION
 
The Committee notes that DG Shipping is the competent authority and equipped with enough paraphernalia to handle
 the security matters as maintained in the Merchant Shipping Act 1958.  The Committee feels that the security concerns
 are growing day by day and there is a need to institutionalize the security element.  The Committee therefore,
 recommends that, even if, the DG Shipping oversees the functions, for securing maritime environment, there should be
 a Maritime Security Advisory Committee to deal with security matters and to make recommendation on National
 Maritime Security issues.
 (Para 29)
SECTION 3 (44A) (ii)
The Committee is not in agreement with the replies furnished by the Department of Shipping. The Committee is of the
 view that the terms "Against any other hostile act or influence" as mentioned in chapter II, Section 3, Sub-Section 44A
 (ii) is too broad and therefore open to an interpretation.  The Committee feels that a good law must be very specific and
 should properly define the acts of violation otherwise it can be misused against anybody. The Committee therefore,
 recommends that the Department of Shipping should clearly specify and incorporate "any other hostile act or influence"
 in the Bill itself so as to make it more comprehensive and subject to monitoring.
 (Para 33)
SECTION 344L and 344Q
 
The Committee is not satisfied with the reply of the Department of Shipping.  The Committee is of the firm opinion that
 the term 'such other authority' in Section 344L and 344Q for the purpose of issue of ship identification number and
 international ship security certificate is vague and requires specific mention in the act itself.  The Committee feels that
 flexibility for delegation of authority may further lead to its misuse and as a result of which the security may be
 compromised.  The Committee therefore recommends that the term 'such other authority' should be defined in the Act

 (Para 35)
SEAMEN IDENTITY DOCUMENT
 
The Committee notes that the Department of Shipping is in the process of establishing necessary infrastructure for
 issuance of the Seamen Identity Document without causing any harassment to the seafarers since it is the most vital
 document which establishes the genuineness and the identity of the Seamen.  However, the Committee feels that there
 is definitely a necessity to rationalize the method of issuance of identification  document.  The Committee recommends
 the Department of Shipping to rationalize the method of issuing identification document in a completely transparent
 and objective manner without leaving any scope for its subjective application in the future.
 (Para 37)

 Seamen working below 500 gross tonnage vessels in the name of security risk.  However, the Committee notes that the
 proviso to 344J empowers the Central Government to extend the application of ISPS Code to certain ships and port
 facilities and DG Shipping is already seized of the matter.  The Committee recommends that the Department of
 Shipping should revisit the provisions of Section 344J with a view to protect the right of the Seamen and ensure that no
 harassment is caused to the Seamen working in the smaller vessels.

 and legitimate trade union activities should also be incorporated in the bill itself.

 section 344 (M).

INTRODUCTION
 
            I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture,
 having been authorised by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby present this Ninetieth Report on
 “Development of Airport Sector with Special Emphasis on new Modern Airports”.
 
2.      The Committee, at its meeting held on the 8
th September 2004, decided to take up this subject for examination and
 accordingly, heard the Secretary and other officers of the Ministry of Civil Aviation on the 8 th November and 28 th
 December 2004 and 6th June and 29th June 2005.
 
3.      The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the officers of the Ministry of Civil Aviation for placing before the
 Committee the material and information desired in connection with the subject and for clarifying the points raised by
 the Members.
 
4.      The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on the 7th August 2005.
 
New Delhi;
August 17, 2005
Sarvana 26, 1927 (Saka)
Nilotpal Basu
Chairman,
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee
 on Transport, Tourism & Culture.
 
 
R E P O R T
            Airports are the gateways to a nation.  However, in our country, the state of the airports, both domestic and
 international, leaves much to be desired.  The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
 Tourism and Culture discussed the state of airports in the country and was of the opinion that the situation at the
 airports in the country was a cause of concern.  Air travel has registered tremendous growth due to various factors such
 as higher incomes, more corporate activity, low cost airlines, cheaper fares and absence of adequate rail and road
 transport infrastructure.  At a time when the civil aviation sector was taking wings in the country, the airport
 infrastructure in the country had come under tremendous stress.  The infrastructure available at the airports and the
 amenities inside the airports are grossly inadequate and are in urgent need of replacement or modernization. 
 Accordingly, during the last few years, the Government of India had taken some steps for the modernization of airports
 in the country. The steps initiated by the Government for the development/modernization of airport sector in the

90th Report of the Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/90threport.htm[28-08-2018 13:13:41]
 country drew the attention of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and
 Culture and accordingly the Committee decided to take up the various aspects of  'Development of Airport Sector with
 special emphasis on new modern airports' for study and examination.
 
2.         The Committee requested the Ministry of Civil Aviation to furnish a detailed background note on the subject for
 consideration of the Committee.  The Committee also held the oral evidence of the representatives of Ministry of Civil
 Aviation and Airports Authority of India on the 8 th November and 28 th December 2004 and 6 th June and 29 th June
 2005.  The Committee also sought replies to the queries on the subject during the oral evidence of the Secretary and
 other representatives of Ministry of Civil Aviation during the examination of Demands for Grants 2005-06 of the
 Ministry of Civil Aviation.  The various aspects of the subject discussed by the Committee and the Committee's
 observations thereon have been brought out in the succeeding paragraphs of the report.
MODERNISATION AND RESTRUCTURING OF DELHI AND MUMBAI AIRPORTS
 
3.         As per their plans for developmental process of airports, the Ministry of Civil Aviation had taken steps to
 modernize and restructure Delhi and Mumbai airports through Joint Venture route.  The Ministry of Civil Aviation
 provided the following brief consisting of the details of various steps the Government took towards restructuring and
 modernization of Delhi and Mumbai airports:-
 
The Cabinet in its meeting held on 11 th September 2003 accorded its approval for the restructuring of Delhi and
 Mumbai airports by adopting the Joint-Venture route.
 
The AAI Amendment Bill introduced in the Parliament (Budget Session 2003) was passed by the Parliament in
 the Monsoon Session of June 2003.  The Amendment Bill authorizes AAI to transfer the operations and
 management of its existing airports by way of long-term lease to private players.  The Bill inter alia provides for
 exclusion of private airports (like BIAL) from the ambit of AAI Act, excepting security and ATC functions,
 which will continue to be discharged by AAI.  The Bill also authorizes AAI to change Advance Development
 Fee (ADF) for the development/upgradation of existing airports and for the setting up of Greenfield airports.  In
 addition, the Bill also seeks to prevent and remove encroachments of airport land.  The provisions of Airports
 Authority of India (Amendment) Act 2003 became effective w.e.f. 1 st July 2004, as per Gazette Notification
 dated 1st July 2004. 
 
The Cabinet constituted an Empowered Group of Ministers (EGOM) to take up decisions on various issues
 connected with the restructuring of Mumbai and Delhi airports. In this connection the Cabinet also decided to
 constitute an Inter-Ministerial Group (IMG) to assist EGOM.  The IMG was accordingly constituted by Ministry
 of Civil Aviation during October 2003 under the Chairmanship of Additional Secretary & Financial Advisor of
 MCA and other Members from the MCA, MoF, Department of Disinvestment and Ministry of Law, Justice &
 Company Affairs and AAI.
 
To assist Ministry of Civil Aviation (MOCA)/Airports Authority of India (AAI) in the restructuring process, AAI
 invited technical & financial bids for the appointment of Financial Consultants.  M/s. ABN AMRO were selected
 as Financial Consultants and they started the work in January 2004.
 
After obtaining the approval of EGOM, Registration of Expressions of Interest were solicited from interested
 parties to acquire 74% equity state in the JVC and the complete documentation, in this regard, was uploaded in
 the websites of AAI and MCA on 17.02.2004.  The last date for submission of EOI was 04.06.2004.
 
Subsequent to formation of the new Government, the Hon'ble Minister of State for Civil Aviation discussed in

90th Report of the Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/90threport.htm[28-08-2018 13:13:41]
 detail few critical issues relating to the Transaction including the quantum of foreign direct investments.  In order
 to address these critical issues, the last date of submission of Expression of Interest was extended to 20 th July
 2004.
 
The Cabinet in its meeting held on 15 th June 2004 reconstituted the EGOM under the Chairmanship of Defence
 Minister to take the Transaction forward.
 
The reconstituted EGOM has, inter-alia, approved the 49% cap of FDI, restriction of equity participation by
 Indian Scheduled Airlines upto 10% increasing the deputation period of employees in the JVCs from 2 to 3 years
 and also decided to give weightage to bidders who will induct more number of employees over and above the
 mandatory induction of 40% net.
 
The EGOM also approved the appointment of M/s. Airplan, Australia as the Global Technical Advisor and M/s.
 Amarchand & Mangaldas Suresh A. Shroff as legal Consultant.
 
Ten entities have lodged their EOIs by 20th July 2004 (i.e. last date of the receipt of EOIs).  Evaluation of EOIs is
 on hand.  
 
Subsequent to the approval of the Board of AAI, M/s. Thakur, Vaidyanath Aiyar & Co. has been appointed an
 Accounting and Tax Advisor for the Transaction and they have since started their assignment.
 
4.         The Committee desired to know from Ministry of Civil Aviation as to what was meant by modernization of
 these airports.  In response, the Committee was informed by Ministry that the modernization of these airports would
 mean the attainment/achievement of the key strategic objectives of the Government of India as envisaged for the
 transaction, which are as under:
 
(i)                  World Class development and expansion - Under this objective, a world-class phased
 development/expansion is contemplated through timely provision of high quality airport infrastructure
 on both airside and landside to meet growing traffic demands.
 
(ii)                World Class airport management - Under this objective, a world class airport management team and
 systems is contemplated by selection of successful bidders with suitable operational experience,
 managerial and financial capability, financial commitment and the commitment to provide quality
 airport service.
 
5.         In addition to the key Transaction objectives, other Transaction objectives include:
·        Timely completion and certainty of closure, with minimal residual risks;
·        Smooth transition of operations, under concession agreements;
·        Appropriate regulation-achieving economic regulation of aeronautical assets that is fair, commercially and
 economically appropriate,  transparent, predictable, consistent and stable while protecting the interest of
 users and ensuring that the Airports are operated in accordance with world standards;
 
·        Fair and equitable treatment of AAI employees, including preservation of accrued entitlement; and
 
·
        Diversity of ownership between Delhi and Mumbai airports, to enhance competition, encourage innovation
 and allow competitive benchmarking.

6.         During the course of oral evidence of the Meeting held on 8 th November 2004, the Secretary, Ministry of Civil
 Aviation while giving details of development of airport sector in the country informed the Committee as under:-
           
"We have estimated that Delhi and Mumbai Airports would require an investment of roughly
 around Rs.10,000/- to Rs.20,000/- crore .  There are 23 smaller airports which would require an
 investment of around Rs.5000/- each.  The Greenfield airports would requirement of Rs.3,596 crore."
 
7.         The Committee was surprised to note the statement of the Secretary that as per their estimates, Delhi and
 Mumbai airports would require an investment of Rs.10,000 to Rs.20,000 crore.  The Committee, therefore, desired to
 know the budget cost estimates for modernization and restructuring of Delhi and Mumbai airports.  The Ministry of
 Civil Aviation vide their O.M. No.H-11013/3/2004-AAI dated 12th January 2005 informed the Committee that so far as
 Mumbai airport was concerned, based on the study carried out by the Financial Consultant appointed by Airports
 Authority of India, the annual aircraft movement is expected to grow up from 151,000 movements in 2004 to 500,000
 movements in 2024 and correspondingly the annual passenger movement is expected to go up from 14 million in 2004
 to 52 million in 2024.  This increase in traffic will call for airfield capacity enhancement as also enhancement in
 terminal capacity.  As per the staged development plan worked out by M/s. Airplan Limited, Australia (Global
 Technical Adviser appointed by AAI), the budget cost estimates in respect of Mumbai Airport is of the order of
 Rs.6300 crore for the period from 2005-2019.
 
8.         As regards Delhi Airport, based on the study carried out by the Financial Consultant appointed by Airports
 Authority of India, the annual aircraft  movement is expected to grow up from 117,000 movements in 2004 to 402,000
 movements in 2024 and correspondingly the annual passenger movement is expected to go up from 11.2 million in
 2004 to 42.8 million in 2024.  This increase in traffic will call for airfield capacity enhancement as also enhancement in
 terminal capacity.  As per the staged development plan worked out by M/s. Airplan Limited, Australia [Global
 Technical Adviser appointed by Airports Authority of India], the Budget cost estimates in respect of Delhi Airport is of
 the order of Rs.6500 crore for the period from 2005-2024.
 
9.         The Ministry of Civil Aviation further informed that while the above estimates have been made by the Global
 Technical Adviser (which does not include costs on account of relocation of some existing assets and for removal of
 encroachments), as per the transaction process, the prospective bidders are required to submit their development plans
 taking into account the mandatory facilities to be created in the short-term, which would be prescribed by Airports
 Authority of India/Ministry of Civil Aviation.  The successful bidders will have to submit their master plan within one
 year of their selection, which will be in conformity with the development plans submitted alongwith their bids. 
 Accordingly, the cost estimates as indicated above may undergo appropriate/suitable changes (upward or downward) in
 the light of development plans/master plan of the successful bidders.

 informed the Committee that as per the staged development plan worked out by M/s. Air Plan (Global Technical
 Adviser) the expected traffic at Mumbai has been estimated at 52 million by 2024.  It has been estimated that a cost of
 Approx. Rs.6400 crore need to be incurred in the next 20 years.  Similarly, Delhi is expected to handle 428 million
 passengers by 2024 and investment of approx. Rs.8720 crore is required in the next 20 years.
 
11.       The Committee noted that there was huge difference in the figures quoted by Ministry of Civil Aviation in the
 communications dated 12.1.2005 and 2.3.2005.  The Committee sought a clarification from Ministry of Civil Aviation
 with respect to the difference in figures quoted by them.  In response, the Ministry of Civil Aviation informed the

 Advisor appointed by Airports Authority of India.  Subsequent to further discussions during January & February 2005,

12.       Again, during the oral evidence of the Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation held on 29
th June 2005 the
 Committee expressed surprise at the statement made by the Secretary regarding the quantum of investment estimated
 for development of Delhi and Mumbai airports.  The Secretary, while clarifying the statement made by him on 8 th
 November 2004 regarding the likely investment of Rs.10,000 crore to Rs.20,000  crore for modernization of Delhi and
 Mumbai airports, stated as under:-
 
"I said that tentatively the estimated cost of modernization and development of these airports would be
 around ten to twenty thousand crore.  You had very rightly pointed out that the range was quite wide and
 that it showed that full examination of the question had not taken place.  Since then, there have been a
 number of things that have happened.  We had appointed a global technical advisor, an Australian
 company, which has been working as consultant and advisor to a number of international airports,
 including Hong Kong etc., in Asia.   We tasked them to draw up an initial development plan for Delhi
 and Mumbai, both.  They have now come up with an initial development plan.  I would hasten to add
 here that this is not the final plan.  The final plan will be prepared by the concessionaire who wins the
 bid.  This is an initial development plan prepared by our technical advisers and according to this the
 investment in Delhi Airport is to be done in four stages.  The first stage would commence now. As soon
 as the bidding process is completed by the concession agreements, it will go up to year 2009.  This
 figure of 2009, we have determined keeping in view the hosting by Delhi of the Commonwealth Games
 which are going to be held in 2010.  The second phase would be between 2010 and 2014 and the third
 phase would be between 2015 and 2019.  The fourth phase would be between 2020 and 2024.  By 2024,

15.       The Committee also sought information about the procedure adopted by the Ministry of Civil Aviation for
 executing the development plan for Delhi and Mumbai airports.  During the course of oral evidence held on 29

 2004, the Committee was informed by the Ministry of Civil Aviation that they had invited Expression of Interest (EoI)
 from interested parties for the development of Delhi and Mumbai airports.  Offers were received from ten interested
 parties.  After a process of short-listing, nine parties were identified and request for proposals were issued to these nine
 parties.  The Ministry of Civil Aviation was in the process of issuing these parties the final set of transaction documents
 which had received the approval of the empowered Group of Ministers on 22
nd June 2005.  It was further stated that by
 early August, the bids will come in and then a process of evaluation will start by technically qualified people.  Then,
 revenue sharing will be decided.  When the bids come in, each of the bidders will submit his own plan for development
 of these airports.  The bidder can configure the development plan and find a better way of providing all the facilities.  It

 could be different from what the initial development plan prepared by the Technical Advisor of Ministry of Civil
 Aviation.  Then, they would also do their own estimation.  They would submit those plan, which would be evaluated by
 the Airports Authority of India in consultation with the Technical Adviser.  Ministry of Civil Aviation also stated that

 they were not parking their aircraft there.   The Committee desire to know whether the Government had any mechanism
 to monitor such cases.   In response, the Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation stated as under:
"What we do is that the Airport Authority has allotted a space to them.  The airport belongs to the Airport
 Authority, and the DGCA and the Ministry, before they sanction and proposal of the company, get a
 certificate from the Airport Authority that the company has been allotted one, or maybe two, parking
 spaces, wherever they have undertaken that they have got them.  That cross-check is done."
 
65.       The Committee is of the opinion that exercising vigilance over the new airlines coming up in the country and
 their methods of seeking permission for procurement of aircraft and allotment of parking bays at airports is quite
 essential.  The Committee recommends that the role of all concerned agencies i.e., Airports Authority of India, DGCA,
 etc. in this regard should be closely monitored and compliance of all necessary regulations ensured.

68.       The Committee enquired from the Ministry of Civil Aviation about the conditions stipulated while permitting
 private airlines to operate with regard to making them CAT-III B compliant.  In response, the Committee has been
 informed that as of now, there is no legal requirement in the Aircraft Rules and Civil Aviation Requirements that makes
 it mandatory for private airlines to train their pilots on ILS CAT- III B System.  However, various airlines have been
 coordinated from time to time to train their pilots for using the ILS CAT-III System in order to improve their
 operational efficiency during poor visibility conditions. 
 
69.       The Committee enquired about the details of the Training facilities available with the private airlines and
 monitoring mechanism available with the DGCA, the Ministry of Civil Aviation informed the Committee that the
 private airlines have their own arrangements for training both in ground courses as well as on simulator.  Jet Airways
 have their training establishments at Mumbai excepting simulator training for ATR which is done at Bangkok. 
 Similarly, Sahara Airlines has arrangements with Alteon, U.K. for both ground and simulator training on Boeing type
 aircraft and at CAE Facility, Spain for CRJ-200 aircraft.  Air Deccan carries out both ground and simulator training for
 their pilots on Airbus-320 and ATR aircraft at the Aircraft Manufacturer’s Facility at Toulouse, France.  These training
 facilities are initially approved by the DGCA based on their quality and capacity of training and on the basis of the
 approval of the state in which these establishments are located.  The training establishments in India are also
 periodically inspected by DGCA officers in the course of Safety Audits, Main Base Inspections and other surveillance
 activities.
 
70.       The Committee is constrained to note that on the one hand, the Government has cited resource crunch as the
 prime reason for inviting private sector participation in modernization of airports while on the other hand, the costly
 technologies installed at the airports after making huge investments remain idle due to want of trained personnel.  Also
 while the current policy of the Government aims at allowing more and more airlines to operate in the country, it has not
 made it obligatory for them to utilize the modern facilities installed at the airports with huge investments for the
 convenience of the passengers.  The Committee is surprised to note that the three private airlines i.e. Jet Airways,
 Sahara Airlines and Air Deccan have not trained any of their pilots for CAT-III operations and there is no legal
 requirement in the Aircraft Rules and Civil Aviation requirements to make it mandatory for private airlines to train their
 pilots on ILS CAT-III System.  The Committee is also not satisfied with the progress achieved with respect to the
 training of the pilots by the National Carriers viz. Indian Airlines and Air India, for utilizing the CAT-III System.  The
 Committee recommends that in order to improve the operational efficiency during the extreme foggy conditions, the
 Ministry should amend 'Aircraft Rules' to incorporate a provision for making training of pilots compulsory by the
 private airlines on CAT-III System so that the investment made by the Government on the installation of the system
 through the tax payers' money is not underutilized.  The Committee hopes that the national carriers and the private

71.       The Committee also sought details regarding the development on non-metro airports in the country.  The
 Ministry of Civil Aviation submitted a brief on the subject which stated that a concept paper was circulated by Ministry
 of Civil Aviation in August 2002 for city side development of Non-Metro Airports.  The proposal envisaged that entire
 operational area i.e. runway, taxiway, apron, communication & navigation aids, Air Traffic Management will remain
 with Airports Authority of India.  The expenditure incurred thereon and the revenue earned thereof shall be that of
 Airports Authority of India.  The city side of the airports i.e. non-operational areas which include the terminal building,
 car park, entire area outside the operational boundary wall will only be taken up for development.  The security and
 safety of viable Non-Metro Airports will continue with Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS), Government of
 India and Airports Authority of India and will be maintained as per Government of India guidelines.

 Institution/State Government for city side development of viable Non-Metro Airports.
